As an individual with extensive experience in this field since the early 1990s and also having the privilege of serving on a committee tasked with defining open data structures, I'll draw from my personal knowledge to outline the essential characteristics, classifications, and criteria that distinguish data as open. Furthermore, I'll discuss the required actions from both governments and private organizations to successfully implement and leverage these principles.

Building on previous research, we extend the findings about the properties of Jacobian varieties in generic hyperelliptic curves when perturbed by specific type one Richelot isogenies. This study introduces an extended version of these isogenies, referred to as decomposed Richelot isogenies, and examines their impact on a family of Jacobian varieties resulting from the resolution of singularities. We further identify an innovative method for constructing curves on a generic hyperelliptic K3 surface where these isogenies induce a combination of elliptic displacements and level raising, while applying a generalized version of the Howe curve decomposition technique.

Recent studies have confirmed the existence of magnetic hot subdwarf stars, however the cause behind their magnetic properties remains a contentious issue. The recent discovery of three magnetically active hot subdwarf stars (SDSS 121218.62+140523, SDSS J205953.79+001433.2 and SDSS J163935.52+501054.1) presents a novel scenario in which these fields are generated. The optical and X-ray spectra of these stars have been analyzed and found to be consistent with other magnetic hot subdwarbs discovered previously. The stars' magnetic field strength has been estimated to be within the range of 1-300 millitesla. The examination of these stars' optical and X-ray spectra has led to the suggestion that they may have originated from binary star mergers. The X-ray variability observed in SDSS 121218.62+140523 and SDSS J163935.52+501054.1 provide evidence that these magnetic fields may have been generated during the merger process.

We examine the task of identifying the matrix with the lowest rank that fulfills the given matrix observations. These observations come from measuring the matrix entries with some level of uncertainty. Our focus is on positive semi-definite symmetric matrices, for which we have developed a method that combines Gaussian elimination and matrix matrix multiplication. This approach is based on an algorithm that selects the matrix entries with the highest probability of being non-zero. Our method has been proven to have a high probability of being accurate, achieving an error rate close to the theoretical limit. Through simulations, we have shown that our method performs better than other popular methods.

This paper introduces WikiHist.html, a comprehensive collection of English Wikipedia revisions stored in HTML format, and outlines its usefulness for historical query processing and learning tasks. It is derived from the Wikipedia History dataset, which contains the full revision history of Wikipedia in a semi-structured format known as mediawiki-formats. To address previous limitations, WikiHist.html was created by transforming the original data into a structured HTML format, enabling researchers to pre-process and analyze Wikipedia revisions more efficiently using web browsers and their rendering engines. This dataset offers several advantages, including being easily accessible to various groups, including those without technical expertise. Comprehensive experiments were conducted using natural language processing techniques to analyze the new dataset, highlighting its potential for supporting both interactive and programmatic tasks. WikiHist.html is available for download at https://github.com/leegh0203/WikiHist.

The formation of polar meron-antimeron frameworks is a common occurrence in certain moiré materials, which is also observed in a model of a twisted bilayer with a moiré periodic potential. This phenomenon is particularly noticeable when there is a significant difference in the on-site potential of the two layers. In the context of a model with a moiré periodic potential, the interaction between the two layers is required to be sufficiently attractive for the phenomenon to occur. The meron-antimeron lattice exhibits a topological gap that is determined by the difference in on-site potential and the overlap integral between the two layers. The topological gap is also influenced by the exchange coupling between the two layers, which can be controlled by adjusting the twist angle, while the spatially varying phase of the order parameter can exhibit a gapless mode, a Higgs mode, under a superfluid long-range order between the two layers in the system.

In accordance with the Einstein cosmological model, we are examining the universe's non-planar, spherical shape. We are exploring how this spherical geometry alters the fundamental principles of classical physics, drawing inspiration from the work of M. Lichnerovici. The implications of these changes will be evaluated within the context of gravitational physics, while maintaining the validity of conservation laws. The modifications will be applied to both point-like and extended particles, with particular emphasis on the latter due to their broader physical relevance. We will also consider the implications of these spherical deformities for the concept of space as a background structure, as well as the corresponding changes to the notion of spacetime.

A novel technique for propelling colloids in liquid crystals has been developed using an innovative method that capitalizes on the unique properties of nematic liquid crystals when interacting with surfaces. By carefully controlling the spacing between the surface and a low-order surface structure, colloids can be guided along specific paths determined by the surface topology. Adjustable barriers formed from photonic crystals created through interference patterns enable the guidance of colloids over varying distances and allow for the suppression of unwanted diffusion and rotation. The adjustable colloidal paths are versatile and can be designed to suit a range of applications, including the assembly of microstructures and the fabrication of submicron features.

This study examines how elongated asteroid shapes affect the stability of their outer layers during close approaches with other celestial bodies. We created a numerical model to simulate and analyze the dynamics of a rubble-pole asteroid and its outer layer, and we found that its rotation and the angle of its outer layer's rotation relative to its outer layer's axis influence the stability of its outer layer. We discovered that when asteroids with certain rotation speeds and dimensions encounter other celestial bodies, their outer layers can become unstable, leading to mass loss. This mass loss was found to be more likely to occur when asteroids with certain dimensions encounter other celestial bodies, and our findings suggest that this instability is particularly common among asteroids with elliptical cross-sections.

To design new drugs effectively, understanding protein dynamics in detail is crucial, especially how structural changes influence the protein's behavior. Current supercomputers struggle to analyze complex systems like dynamic proteins, especially those requiring electrostatic simulations. Yet, quantum computers have the potential to overcome these challenges by providing more accurate simulations. Currently, quantum approaches often produce random samples of protein structures, but this can be problematic since many generated states might not represent the actual system well. To address this issue, we propose a new method that adjusts the quantum sampling process to focus on rare, low-energy protein structures, which are more representative of the actual system. Our approach is demonstrated using the 130-nanosecond Lennard-Jones MD simulation of protein GB1.

A novel Monte Carlo code, called MAPPIES, has been developed to model inverse external Compton scattering involving partially polarized synchrotron radiation. This code can account for radiation polarization in the inverse external Compton scattering process, taking into account not only electron-photon interactions, but also electron scattering against circularly polarized photons. MAPPIES includes radiation models, like those of Kurucz and Voit, to simulate synchrotron radiation, and an optical model to simulate complex light interactions. This code can be applied to diverse contexts including astrophysics, particle physics and laser studies. By simulating these interactions, electron and photon energy spectra are calculated, and electron distribution functions are determined. This code can be applied to various astrophysical contexts like active galactic nuclei, hot spots, and shocks. By simulating radiation interactions, MAPPIES can be applied to diverse contexts including astrophysics, hot plasma studies, and laser-based particle accelerators. This code can be used to simulate radiation interactions, and study electron and photon energy spectra in various astrophysical contexts. By simulating these interactions, the proposed code can be applied to diverse particle physics contexts, and help study laser-based particle accelerators.

The Arctic Ocean's thin ice is a result of multi-year ice's reduced store over several seasons. This study utilizes a three-layer ice model with a focus on the thickness distribution's evolution. It shows that the ice's aging process can be described using a limited number of effective parameters, derived from a set of simplified equations, that accurately capture the seasonal shifts in ice thickness distribution. These parameters are found to be consistent with the findings of in-situ measurements, and model data from the Pan-Arctic SHEBA region, indicating that the thickness distribution's seasonal changes can be effectively reproduced.
In this research, we explore the generalized Weierstrass semigroup at specific points on particular maximal curves that are not encompassed by the classical Hermitian curve.

This paper conducts an in-depth examination of cutting-edge deep learning techniques used in singing voice synthesis systems. The main objective is to provide a thorough understanding and offer recommendations for selecting the most suitable deep learning approach for a specific application. The review encompasses recent advancements in singing voice synthesis, incorporating both generative and discriminative methods. We explore the deep learning techniques used in modeling the acoustic representation of speech, in both the short-term (short-time Fourier analysis) and long-term (mel-spectrogram) domains. The proposed models either rely on pre-trained neural networks or train the models from scratch, and are either end-to-end or require external training data, such as text or mel-spectrogram. We also analyze non-end-to-end training approaches, including voice conversion and manipulation techniques. Ultimately, the performance of the models is evaluated through objective and subjective assessments.

Our Birdsong Dataset, NIPS4Bplus, is an exceptionally annotated audio collection, featuring approximately 50 bird species and over 4,000 bird samples. This dataset is equipped with an extensive range of annotations, including raw audio, spectrograms, mel-spectrograms, bird identification, location information, and more than 300 detailed tracks containing sound activity, song types, and ground truth melodies. NIPS4Bplus is built on bird conservation datasets, bird sounds databases, and Google Knowledge, and is designed to support bird species classification, identification, and recognition tasks, as well as machine listening applications. A web-based interface provides users with a user-friendly interface to explore and download dataset content, and the dataset is accessible via the bird-conservation.org website.

Time-resolved image arrays, known as event cameras, possess a unique quality of measuring both temporal changes in light intensity and spatial locations of photons, with the added benefit of having low power consumption. These capabilities make them suitable for applications in fields like machine vision, robotics, and surveillance. Despite their advantages, event cameras are often plagued by spatial and temporal distortions in their images due to factors such as their rectangular photodiodes and low frame rates. These distortions can be particularly problematic when working with intricate scenes that require high spatial and temporal resolution to accurately identify events. In this research, we introduce a method to rectify these distortions, which involves leveraging the event camera's built-in time information to accurately localize events in both space and time. These corrections enable us to produce undistorted images that closely resemble those captured by high-frame rate cameras. This approach is demonstrated using images from various event cameras, including the event camera PDA4521 from Intersil and the Event Camera Company's EV76U1K4O.

The increasing complexity and interconnected nature of systems and processes in various fields have led to a growing interest in graph analytics as a solution to address these complex relationships. Graph analytics leverages graph data to gain insights into complex patterns within data, making it a valuable tool for discovering hidden structures. Despite its potential, implementing graph analytics can be a daunting task, particularly for organizations with limited experience. A thorough understanding of the graph analytics process and its various components is essential for successful graph analytics implementation. In this article, we provide a comprehensive review of the current graph analytics landscape, covering its applications, challenges, and key considerations. We also offer a future-oriented discussion on the potential evolution of graph analytics and the opportunities that lie ahead.

In this study, we have examined the high-energy collisions of two $\Lambda$ hyperons at $2.83~\mathrm{A}\mathrm{MeV}$ energy level using the $^{4}_{\Lambda }$He $\to ^{4}_{\Lambda }H$ excitation cross-section data. Our findings indicate that the $0^{-}~2^{+}$ and $1^{-}~2^{+}$ states in $^{12}_{\Lambda }C$ are more stable than those in $^{12}_{\Lambda }N$, whereas the $1^{--}~2^{+}$ and $0^{++}~0^{++}$ states are not significant in both cases. Furthermore, we have suggested that the $^{16}_{\Lambda }C$ and $^{16}_{\Lambda }N$ excitation cross-sections follow a $1^{-}~2^{+}$ state in $^{16}\mathrm{N}$.

In ocular surgery, a notable challenge is navigating a long-scope endoscope within the confined eye cavity. We've devised a new approach to aid the surgeon's device navigation using visible highlights within the eye cavity obtained through endoscopic imaging. Initially, a detailed understanding of the eye cavity is established using a dataset of randomly captured views. Subsequently, a probabilistic algorithm is utilized to create a comprehensive, 3D structure of the eye cavity based on the captured highlights. We've developed a new method to enable the surgeon's device to seamlessly merge captured highlights into a consistent, unified 3D environment, thereby facilitating smooth and efficient device movement within the eye cavity. Our results from a controlled experiment demonstrate that the enhanced visual environment effectively guides the surgeon's device, thereby reducing the number of failed device placements at a rate of 7.2%.

The f-quantum mechanics is an extension of the standard quantum mechanics that employs operators representing the direction of vectors "F", rather than the standard position and momentum operators. The theory's wave function is complex-valued f-function that depends on the position and momentum. Two equations describing the time-evolved wave function after an initial state are derived in the f quantum mechanics. These equations are solved for wave functions in a Gaussian distribution and in a double-Gaussian distribution, and their solutions are analyzed.

The FIDO2 passkey technology, used for passwordless authentication, has been touted as a potential replacement for authentication methods like two-factor authentication and biometrics. However, despite its growing popularity, there are concerns about FIDO2's effectiveness in protecting user privacy. To address these concerns, our paper examines the FIDO2 passkey technology from a privacy perspective. We employ a combination of formal and informal approaches to analyze potential privacy risks associated with FIDO2's implementation in websites. Our research reveals that FIDO2's reliance on third-party browser storage can compromise user privacy by exposing sensitive information. Moreover, we found that FIDO2's reliance on secure online storage and frequent updates can lead to increased overhead and privacy risks. Our research contributes to a better understanding of FIDO2's implications for user privacy, providing valuable insights for developers and users worldwide.

The Weyl transform provides a tool to convert functions between momentum space and real space in solid-state physics, drawing inspiration from Glauber's coherent states theory. It offers an alternative approach to the time-frequency analysis of signals, utilizing a discrete fourier transform like method. We explore the connection between the Weyl transform and lattice dynamical systems, highlighting its similarity to the second quantization method used in path integral techniques. We also discuss the potential for the Weyl transform in quantum gravity research, specifically in creating coherent states of the gravitational field on a lattice.

This research investigates how the layout of YouTube's homepage influences individuals' sense of control, particularly in relation to control theory predictions. We discovered that when algorithm-driven recommendations occupy more screen space, it diminishes users' feelings of control. Conversely, allowing users to set a preferred content category and displaying it on an sizable portion of the screen lets them maintain a greater sense of control. We explored how different user preferences might impact their sense of control when confronted with algorithm-driven recommendations versus user-navigated content choices. Lastly, our findings suggest that empowering users with the choice between algorithm-driven and user-driven content experiences could be a powerful method for boosting users' feelings of control.

We establish that the proof of a process in the π-calculus being Turing complete can be transformed into a code running within a polytime bounded context, thereby giving the π-calculus a practical completeness status. This theoretical finding is then combined with the concept of process orchestration to prove that every specifiable behavior by a system described in the π-calculus can also be achieved through a symmetrical, repetitive, and hierarchical execution pattern known as orbit-finite executability.

Permutation numbers of arranged trees have unimodular census numbers, making them ideal for analysis using unimodular group actions. We apply the S1-wreath action to arrange trees in S1-wreath cosets of the edge set. By analyzing this nested action, we establish a gray code structure on these arranged trees. Additionally, using the S1-wreath action allows us to create a bijection between the S1-wreath cosets and rooted, centrally balanced trees, facilitating efficient enumeration of arranged trees.

The sPHENIX detector at RHIC is set to begin experiments in 2022, focusing on studying the quark-gluon plasma. A primary aspect of this research involves investigating the initial stages of heavy-ion collisions. A crucial component of this investigation is measuring two-particle correlation functions within the first millisecond following collision. To achieve this, sPHENIX's detector design incorporates multiple tracking systems, including a Large-Area Time Projection Chamber and a Muon-Dedector. A software framework called ACTS has been developed to simulate the tracking system's expected performance by simulating particle tracks based on real-world conditions. To further enhance accuracy, a new simulation component was introduced, specifically designed to model the Large-Area Time Projection Chamber's functionality and data creation. To streamline and enhance data processing within the trajectory reconstruction framework, a new module named TPC3d was created. This module generates three-dimensional tracks based on single or multiple two-dimensional projections and allows for efficient data filtering based on various criteria. A new physics selection module was also introduced, further enabling detailed analysis of the initial stages of heavy-ion collisions through generated data.

A widely used approach in the finite element time integration of Hamilton's principle is the time-step discretization of the space-time finite element method. This approach typically involves transforming the strong form into a weak form and integrating the time-dependent terms, including the double integral of the time derivative of the trial function and the time-integrated form of the residual. This time integration can be accomplished using various methods, such as the backward Euler, implicit Euler, or trapezoidal rule. To handle time-dependent material derivatives, the space-time finite element method must incorporate a non-standard treatment of the time direction. This can be achieved by employing the vectorial form of integration by parts in space, which results in nonstandard integration in time. This research focuses on the time integration of the time-dependent terms using various methods, such as Euler's rule and the trapezoidal rule. It also addresses the treatment of the time-dependent material derivatives, which is typically overlooked in existing literature. To handle the time-direction integration, the research introduces a new approach that leverages the nonstandard integration in space, which is a typical characteristic of the space-time finite element method. This research also explores the treatment of the time-direction integration of the time-dependent material derivatives, which is a crucial aspect of the space-time finite element method. It provides a new approach to handle the time-direction integration of the time-dependent material derivatives, which is a non-standard procedure.

This study delves into the concept of circular currents in a closed network with a specified number of nodes, $n$, and mono-directional edges carrying positive or negative signs. A notable discovery was that a circular loop with uniformly assigned signs would be stable if and only if the number of nodes is even and the total signed weight is an even multiple of $2i$. This paper further explores the behavior of circular currents in networks where the signs are determined by a directed path. It demonstrates that if a network admits a circular loop, it also supports a circular current with the same starting point, but with the opposite orientation. Additionally, we establish a criterion for determining whether a network supports a stable circular current by analyzing its graph structure.

We propose a probabilistic algorithm that, given a set of n elements and the subset S, can identify all elements in Subsets of S in O(2^n) time with a constant probability of success. Additionally, we introduce a deterministic algorithm that can identify all elements in O(2^n) time. Both algorithms operate in a specific model, where access to elements in S is restricted and not individual set elements are accessible directly. Our proposed algorithms provide a solution to solve the complete problem of identifying all elements in S, given the solution to the partial problem of identifying the emptiness of S.

A recent study of the ASAS-SN light curves revealed 13 light curves exhibiting characteristics of 8 distinct burst events from 8 different stars. These burst events encompass a range of phenomena, including a previously documented outburst and a newly identified variable star. The light curves of the bursts can be classified into three distinct types, based on their temporal duration and shape. The first type, characterized by a gradual decline in the light curve, features a steep initial drop of up to 2 magnitudes, followed by a decline in approximately 100 days. The second type, exhibiting a similar initial decrease but with a flatter slope, takes longer to reach its peak brightness. The light curves of the third type, however, display a rapid increase in the light emitted by these stars, along with a longer duration of brightening. These light curves can be identified by their initial increase in the light emitted by these stars, with a steep slope that reaches a peak brightness over the course of a few days. The light curves of the third type, however, display a gradual decline in the light emitted by these stars, with a slope that is less steep.

In Drosophila melanogstra embryos, hemocytes exhibit unusual movement characteristics during a critical early stage. Unlike typical ameboid motion, hemocyte movement demonstrates minimal directional persistence over time, indicating a lack of chemotactic persistence. Furthermore, the dynamic movement of hemocytes is distinct from that of migrating cells in the immune response, exhibiting instead characteristics of solid-body rotation. Moreover, the dynamic movement of hemocytes is not due to changes in the cytoskeleton, as experiments have shown that cytoskeletal remodeling is non-essential for their dynamic movement. The unique characteristics of hemocyte movement in the Drosophila embryo suggest a previously unexplored mechanism for cell movement.

Recent advancements in computer vision have led to the development of semi-supervised learning techniques that minimize the use of labeled data, as demonstrated by Siamese Network-based methods. Inspired by these innovations, researchers have explored similar approaches for speech recognition, with promising results. However to date, there have been limited evaluations and assessments of Siamese Network-based methods for speech recognition using large, publicly available datasets. This paper introduces a novel Siamese Network approach that incorporates both labeled and unlabeled speech data, with an emphasis on comparing and evaluating its performance in various training scenarios. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed method, the researchers utilized the large-scale LibriSpeech and MS-CDIP datasets, yielding notable improvements in speech recognition accuracy, specifically +2.2% and +2.8% respectively, when compared to the traditional, fully supervised training approach.

A detailed report detailing the development of a tool for unresponsive framework functions in lepton-nucleon scattering, as well as its accompanying implementation, is presented. This report also outlines the methodology for generating framework functions' transverse responses from their unresponsive counterparts, a novel method that diverges from established procedures in the field.

This paper addresses the adaptive management of complex systems that switch between different modes, with the goal of achieving the best possible performance. A key aspect of this problem is that the underlying mode sequence is unknown and must be estimated adaptively. To address this challenge, we develop a new method that combines two main components. First, we utilize a specific filtering approach to improve the estimation of the current mode, which is then used to inform a control strategy that maximizes performance. Our main theoretical result shows that this approach leads to nearly certain stabilization, meaning that the probability of this method stabilizing the system approaches 100% as time evolves. Specifically, under certain conditions, the system can be effectively managed as if the underlying mode sequence were known, with the estimated mode converging to the actual one almost surely.

A growing body of evidence suggests that the human brain processes the world around us by actively seeking out relevant information through exploration and processing of that information. However, current methods of active learning used in neuroscience and machine learning typically rely on a single sensory input or a fixed set of sensors. To address this limitation, we have developed a new model called M3-BT-AI, which accounts for multiple sensory modalities and adaptive information-seeking behavior. This model is based on a unified theory called active inference, but with the ability to choose which sensory modality to explore and process at any given time. To evaluate the effectiveness of our model, we have tested it on a navigation task in a simulated virtual environment using visual and vestibular cues, demonstrating improved performance with the active learning approach compared to a more passive method.

We investigate how a KdV soliton evolves in a quark-gluon plasma, with the goal of understanding how different particle species affect the soliton's behavior. By incorporating energy and momentum conservation laws, we derive a basic equation that governs the soliton's behavior and analyze its implications across various conditions. Our analysis reveals that the solion's speed remains stable across different particle species, with the notable exception of a slight decrease in temperature-dependent scenarios. Furthermore, our results indicate that the inclusion of strange quarks causes a minor decrease in the soliton's speed and significantly, the inclusion of light quarks results in a substantial speed decrease. These findings are significant because they demonstrate that the inclusion of certain particle species can have a substantial impact on the solion's behavior.

This research delves into the properties of specific topological vector spaces and develops criteria for when a locally convex space can be classified as Eberlein-Grothendieck. The study also explores the Eberlein-Grothendieck property in the context of dual spaces and establishes that a bornological space is Eberlein-Grothendieck if and only if its dual space has this same property.

This study delves into the concept of isochronicity within a system that consists of a solitary degree of freedom governed by elastic energy plus a time-dependent, potential-based forcing mechanism. Our investigation is rooted in the fact that this particular system serves as the one-dimensional foundation for the two-dimensional Chirikov resonances. Our key findings can be broken down into two primary components. Firstly, we demonstrate that isochronicity is indeed achievable in systems characterized by solitary degrees of freedom and that this phenomenon is contingent upon the specific characteristics of the associated forcing potential. Secondly, our research reveals that isochronicity is contingent on the initial phase of the forcing mechanism, resulting in a periodic pattern of isochronicity.

A novel, low-dimensional representation, termed the resemblance signature (RS), has been developed to represent a given high-dimensional system, like an attractor or a periodic orbit, by reducing the dimensionality effectively. This signature is obtained by iteratively applying a set of vector-valued functions on the system's time-evolving trajectory. This signature serves as a simplified, low-dimensional model of the original system, and its application has been proven useful in identifying and distinguishing different periodic orbits even within the same chaotic system. Moreover, RS has been shown to be resilient to noise and varying time-resolution of the system's trajectory, and its dimensionality can be adjusted to match available computational resources. This study examines the use of RS to create periodic orbits in the Lorenz system, and it is demonstrated that RS can be utilized as a tool to either identify existing periodic orbits or generate new ones.

The paper investigates a SDE driven by Lévy processes and examines the local asymptotic normality (LAN) criterion in relation to families of distributional parameters, which encompass both the diffusion coefficient's characteristic function and the distribution of the driving Lévy process. It further shows that for non-trivial cases, the LAN criterion is equivalent to the joint LAN criterion for the underlying Lévy measure and characteristic function. Additionally, it explores the LAN criterion in infinite-dimensional parameter spaces, characterizing them with the characteristic function of the underlying Lévy process and finds that the LAN criterion is equivalent to the joint LAN criterion for the underlying Lévy measure.

This note establishes a specific value for $\lambda_{min}(L_f)$, the minimum eigenvalue of the twisted Laplacian associated with a holomorphic flow $f$ within the Teichmüller depiction outlined in [EL3], which effectively serves as an alternative proof of a related finding presented in [EL1]. Furthermore, it is also demonstrated that a corresponding distance measurement has a direct relationship with the size of a specific hyperbolic space region surrounding the Teichmüller curve.

Standard transformers have the drawback of needing to compute the entire context space as input for sequence modeling, which can be a major issue for applications like autoregressive speech synthesis. Researchers have turned to parametric representations as an alternative, but these come with their own set of limitations. A new approach has emerged in the form of non-parametric models like the FNet, which use the Fourier Transform as a mechanism for information processing. However, these models have their own set of drawbacks, including high computational expenses and difficulties in fine-tuning. Our solution to these problems is a new model called FNetAR, which combines the benefits of parametric models with the Fourier Transform's non-parametric capabilities. Our model features two distinct Fourier Transform architectures - one for Fourier parameters and one for Fourier transforms - which are used in combination with tokenization and autoregressive generation. Our experiments have shown that FNetAR significantly outperforms the FNet model in terms of speech synthesis quality and efficiency.

We examine the behavior of GGPDE in the Saez-Ballester theory, which is a theoretical framework in General Relativity. The Saez-Ballester theory is an extension of General Relativity that accommodates a negative cosmological constant and includes unique gravitational elements. The study reveals that the GGPDE model is consistent with recent observational data at various levels of the model's free function $f$, particularly when the model is constrained by both supernovae data and BAO. The model's predictive power is similar to that of other time-dependent DE models. The Saez-Ballester theory is also shown to be in line with recent observational data. The GGPDE model is further investigated in the Saez-Ballester theory, which results in a cosmological solution that is similar to a cosmological constant at early times, followed by cosmic acceleration at late times. The model's behavior is similar to that of $\Lambda$CDM at early times, which is a characteristic of the GGPDE model. The GGPDE model is also examined in the context of the Saez-Ballester theory, which results in a cosmological solution that is consistent with the observed late-time cosmic acceleration. The model's free function is constrained using a combination of BAO, supernovae data, and Hubble data, which results in a prediction of the growth factor at a given set of function values. This research introduces a dynamic pricing model for MEC systems that takes into account task chaining in a multi-user setting. A virtual machine operator seeks to execute a series of tasks at MEC servers, which adjust their internal clock frequencies in response to incoming tasks. The operator aims to minimize overall costs based on both computing and energy expenditures. We establish a pricing framework for MEC servers and analyze the resulting equilibrium pricing scenario. In this model, VMs and MEC servers are represented as distinct agents, which interact through variable prices, allowing the analysis of dynamic pricing strategies. A reinforcement learning algorithm, inspired by mean-field control principles, is then proposed for the virtual machine operator to effectively select suitable MEC servers and minimize total expenses. Experimental findings show that this algorithm performs better than existing approaches both in terms of performance and computational complexity.

Our investigation of the renormalization group (RG) focuses on four-fermion models with a stochastic mass, a type of interaction that's been explored in the context of superfluids. When applying the RG to a theory with a $4-\epsilon$ expansion in $\epsilon = d-4$, we find that the stochastic mass contributes significantly at high energy scales but has a negligible effect at low energy scales. Consequently, it doesn't affect the power-counting behavior of the RG fixed points, a finding that's supported by the RG analysis of large $N$ models with similar interactions.

Individuals who experience depression often struggle to discover joy in life's daily activities. This study delves into the positive experiences of individuals living with depression, providing a more comprehensive understanding of their experiences. Through a qualitative analysis of 51 interviews, our research sheds light on the positive experiences of individuals struggling with depression, allowing us to design more effective support systems. Our findings reveal that joy is present in everyday activities, particularly when connections with others are strong. This includes the support of loved ones, the presence of children, and the pursuit of shared hobbies. Additionally, transitions in life events, such as weddings, and new hobbies, can bring moments of joy. Our study also shows that certain locations, like nature and the ocean, can provide a sense of calm and well-being. Ultimately, our research suggests that joy is present in the mundane, highlighting the importance of designing systems that facilitate a more meaningful and fulfilling depression treatment experience.

We conducted a comprehensive parallel-computation investigation into the confinement phase of symmetric axion theory to derive the dependence of the mass spectrum on lattice spacing and volume, as well as the properties of the pion-particle. A novel hybrid-Defect Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm was employed to overcome the significant barrier preventing standard HMC from efficiently sampling the theory's domain-wall configuration. Our results confirm that the pion-particle's mass adheres to two distinct scaling laws - one related to volume, and the other tied to lattice spacing - and demonstrate that the isospin symmetry disruption exhibits significant lattice spacing dependence. These findings validate the isospin symmetry disruption as a reliable indicator of the confinement phase in symmetric axion theory.

The crystal structure of Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$ (with Ni$^{2+}$ having $S$ = 1) was studied using neutron diffraction and powder diffraction techniques. This investigation found that in the compound's disordered nickel distribution, an unusual form of ferromagnetic interaction exists. This is characterized by a specific arrangement of magnetic moments along the chain-like structure formed by the nickel ions. This is further supported by the compound's observed saturation field and magnetic susceptibility patterns. Additionally, the compound's spin-lattice coupling was observed to be particularly strong as indicated by the significant difference in temperature at which the compound's magnetic and mechanical properties behave differently.

The proliferation of intelligent vehicular networks (IVNs) has led to a significant increase in the demand for high-speed data exchange, necessitating a robust and efficient architecture. In response, the concept of cloud-empowered vehicular ad hoc networks (CVEANS) has been proposed, leveraging AI-driven cloud computing and edge computing to enhance IVN performance. However, the seamless integration of these technologies also raises concerns about data privacy and fairness in CVEANS implementations. This research aims to address these concerns by establishing a trust governance structure (TGS) for CVEANS, which includes the development of a trust model to quantify the influence of various factors on trust and by employing a probabilistic approach to account for uncertainty in the network. A Q-learning based trust evaluation algorithm is also proposed to determine trust scores for CVEANS, which can be used to develop a cloud-based framework for evaluating and fostering trust between vehicles and cloud servers. The efficacy of the proposed TGS is then evaluated through simulations, demonstrating its potential to address trust and fairness concerns in CVEANS environments.

A new cubic spline estimation technique is introduced in this paper to analyze functions with significant gradient changes, specifically those with abrupt changes near a single point. The estimation approach employs a two-dimensional smoothing factor that serves as a parameter, allowing for flexible adjustments to the estimation process. Theoretical evidence supporting the method includes consistency, convergence rates, and optimal mean squared error results. The estimation technique's efficacy is demonstrated through a Monte Carlo study that compares its performance with other estimation methods.

We have found a novel solution to the Einstein equations with a positive cosmological constant and a scalar field whose matter source is non-zero in the deep AdS space but vanishes in the asymptotic future. This spacetime features two NUT charges and shares key properties with the Taub-NUT spacetime but is distinct. It includes a black bounce within the Taub-NUT region and a de Sitter-like behavior in the asymptotic future, while also possessing a de Sitter-like behavior near the bounce. This solution is maximally symmetric at both the de Sitter-like and asymptotically non-compact ends and represents the first instance of a de Sitter-like spacetime with a singularity. We have also examined the scalar field dynamics and thermal stability issues associated with this solution.

Large annotated datasets are required for training deep learning models, but labeling these datasets can be costly in terms of time and mental effort.  To optimize the process of creating these datasets, an iterative process called Interactive Annotated Corpus Generation (IACG) can be employed.  This method allows users to prioritize annotated data creation according to specific criteria, like the number of labels involved, and then provides the most informative examples for each label.  This process reduces the overall cost of annotation by prioritizing the most complex data.  To evaluate the effectiveness of IACG, we implemented it in a Korean dataset for sentiment analysis and observed a 60% reduction in annotation costs compared to a random approach.  Our method is adaptable and can be applied to any annotated corpus, but the success of our specific application depends on the structure of the Korean language and the quality of our domain expert.  We have also made our annotated corpus available for others to use.

We've developed a new dynamic mean-field theory that effectively models
complex reaction networks by simplifying diverse environments into a single
parameter-based framework. This approach, supported by numerical simulations, 
enables us to calculate the average steady-state probability distribution, 
initial conditions, and reaction rates for large-scale systems that are highly 
influenced by noise and spatial variations. This theory also accounts for the 
influence of non-Poisson noise and random environments on reaction rates. 
Notably, our theory demonstrates that the reaction rates in spatial systems 
frequently differ from those in one-dimensional systems and that the steady-state 
fluctuations in spatial systems are smaller than their spatially uniform 
counterparts.

The Cayley graph of a symmetric random matrix group has been found to exhibit
self-similar patterns at the scale of random walks and percolation processes,
with an added layer of universality emerging from the distribution of avalanche sizes in the edge values of the Cayley graph. The set of edge values within the group, when considered, forms a self-similar pattern at larger scales, with the distribution of avalanche sizes in the edge values displaying a unique, universal pattern that is unaffected by specific finite-dimensional matrix group types, converging to a limit determined by the underlying continuum limit percolation model. The same universal patterns are observed in the distribution of vertex and edge values, with a notable distinction arising from the edge distribution displaying distinct one-dimensional scaling properties.

To address the issue of sentence link prediction in Open-Domain Question Answering, we propose a new approach called Discourse Understanding (DU). Our method focuses on learning a query responding mechanism that understands the relationship between sentences, specifically focusing on the context that questions and related answers depend on. Unlike previous methods, our approach captures the discourse between a question and answer by focusing on the underlying structure that connects them, rather than the entire context. We achieve this by developing a query responding network that generates a score indicating how well a given answer choice relates to the question within the surrounding discourse, using a multi-head attention mechanism to extract relevant information from the entire context. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a multi-task training process, utilizing a variety of tasks such as question type prediction and answer position prediction as auxiliary tasks. Our experiments show that DU significantly outperforms existing methods on the HotpotQA dataset, achieving a new state-of-the-art result.

We present a review of recent advancements in the aptly suited layer approach, encompassing the development of a generalized model for hyperbolic wave transmission and relevant mathematical formulations.

A cluster of liquid droplets can be arranged in various patterns and can act as a sensor or sensor array, detecting certain conditions or conditions related to specific events. To create a specific pattern, the interdroplet forces play a crucial role in determining the long-term arrangement. However, the conditions of these forces can be altered by external influences, leading to changes in the droplet configuration. A study investigates the effect of laser pulses striking the droplet cluster, changing their arrangement in the process. A computational model is used to analyze the impact of these pulses, showing that multiple pulses can rearrange the droplet configuration in different ways.

The rapidly expanding Internet of Things (IoT) network is expected to reach a staggering 50 billion connected devices by 2025, generating an enormous amount of data from diverse sources. Although edge computing and Software-Defined Networking (SDN) present a promising solution to manage IoT data, their integration remains a largely uncharted territory. This paper presents a novel data orchestration framework, termed Pub/Sub SDN-enmeshed, which leverages SDN to provide a unified view of IoT devices, dynamic network resources, and data generated within the network. A customized OpenFlow controller and data plane are designed to enable real-time data management and data plane reconfiguration manipulation. A dynamic model is also proposed to efficiently allocate virtual instances of the controller to optimize data management. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through evaluation of data plane reconfiguration and virtual controller instance allocation.

We used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to observe the continuum and molecular lines in this system at 3 mm and 1.3 mm wavelengths. A novel metric, referred to as the metric-induced metric, is introduced, enabling the definition of a vector-valued metric within a specific space. Demonstrating its applicability, a gyrovector calculus for a space of symmetric positive definite matrices is established.

The European Union's goal to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 60% by 2030 sets the stage for a carbon-neutral energy scenario, prompting the question of what role hydrogen could play in meeting this challenge, particularly as the country prepares to host the 2020 World Hydrogen Summit. This article explores the global hydrogen trade, the benefits of using hydrogen produced from natural gas in power generation, the role of hydrogen produced from natural gas in the global power system, and the potential for natural gas to serve as a transition fuel to support the widespread adoption of renewable hydrogen. By examining the global hydrogen trade, the power generation requirements necessary to meet demand from significant hydrogen producers like Norway and the Netherlands can be determined, revealing that these countries could support 40% of hydrogen demand with in-house hydrogen production by 2030, dwarfing the potential of smaller domestic hydrogen producers. Furthermore, the study finds that countries like Germany and China, which are heavily invested in hydrogen production, could meet 60% and 45% of hydrogen demand with their domestic hydrogen supplies. The research also reveals that Germany's hydrogen production capacity is sufficient to power all of London's power needs by 2030, while China's hydrogen production capacity is equivalent to about 20% of the country's power generation capacity. The movement of charged particles from subterranean to surface regions in the Earth's magnetic field is influenced by magnetic field lines and is detectable through magnetic fields and surface currents. This movement is primarily directed by magnetic field lines with the highest strength. The time spent by particles in the tunnel is called travel duration and is dependent on the length of the field line and drift distance. This duration can be shortened by strong magnetic fields and enhanced by surface magnetic fields and surface currents. This paper discusses the relationship between magnetic fields and surface currents and proposes a method to estimate the travel duration anisotropy using a two-dimensional magnetic field and surface current map.

A novel, topological safeguarded illumination (TSI) approach has been developed to overcome the limitations of classical or quantum information spreading in a noisy channel. This approach involves integrating an encoding unit with a uniting cell that can self-reconfigure into various interconnected components. By implementing TSI, the performance of a quantum communication system in the presence of noise has been enhanced, as demonstrated by an improvement in the fidelity of individual photon data from 0.25 to 0.94, along with an accompanying decrease in the channel's entropy rate from 1.32 to -1.94 bits per photon. Furthermore, the benefits of TSI have also been extended to classical communication systems, where it has been shown to safeguard information-gathering capabilities against an adversary attempting to erase data from the uniting cell.

This paper presents a novel algorithm for crafting trajectories that conform to specific path plans, characterized by continuous variation in duration and curvature. Drones, known to exhibit nonlinear responses to acceleration, pose a challenge to trajectory planning due to their difference from the Newtonian dynamics assumed by most existing algorithms. In order to mitigate this issue, a trajectory creation algorithm is proposed, which optimizes the duration of a predefined path segment in an entirely general manner. By minimizing the total acceleration required to traverse the generated trajectory, a solution that is robust to variations in curvature is achieved. A comparative evaluation of the new algorithm with two conventional trajectory creation methods - constant velocity and snap-created trajectories - reveals that it produces sequences of states with the lowest total acceleration, while maintaining a consistent velocity.

This study proposes a new algebraic representation for a specific type of cyclic code. By utilizing this approach, we investigate some properties and a decoding algorithm for this code. Furthermore, we derive some combinatorial results and develop an algorithm to compute a key component of the code's decoding process.

The US government's Snowmass conference brought together the US theoretical particle physics community to create a comprehensive research plan for the USA. A group focusing on community engagement and career pathways developed a report outlining the state of various stages of particle physics careers, the challenges faced by early-career physicists, and proposed solutions, which can be found in a publicly accessible document. This group's effort was well-received by the community, and many of the issues and recommendations have been incorporated into the overall Snowmass plan.

The orientation of W bosons in tbar-t events from 8 TeV proton-proton collisions, studied in the lepton+jets channel by the ATLAS detector at the LHC, is being re-evaluated. Previously, the analysis of W bosons in three dimensions and several related variables led to an indication that their orientation was not uniform, with an anisotropy value of 0.26. However, the method's limitations and uncertainties in jet measurements were seen to be too great to confirm this finding at the 95% confidence level. In an attempt to improve upon this, a new method is being developed that uses a three-dimensional probability distribution model to describe the orientation of W bosons in tbar-t events. This new method utilizes 20.2 fb^-1 of data, significantly increasing the precision of measurements of W orientation.

The $D$-meson twist-3 functions have significant importance for calculating the
cross-sections in neutrino collisions and quasielastic scattering processes.
This research re-examines the calculation methods for these functions, incorporating
the effects of power corrections related to the heavy quark mass, and includes
the influence of a static mass boundary in the D-meson. A comparison is made
between the proposed method of parameter fitting and the results of lattice QCD,
with a re-evaluation of the theoretical uncertainty based on various theoretical
assumptions.

For a given connected graph and its associated hypergraph, we have demonstrated that the spectral radius of the hypergraph is equal to the spectral radius of the graph, following the removal of all even parity edges. Furthermore, we have found that the second largest eigenvalue of the hypergraph corresponds to the second largest eigenvalue of the graph, following the removal of all 4-cycles. We also establish that the second largest eigenvalue of the hypergraph corresponds to the spectral radius of the graph, following the removal of all edges and certain signed structures. Notably, we have demonstrated that the second largest eigenvalue of the hypergraph is directly related to the spectral radius of the graph, following the removal of all edges and certain signed structures. We also establish that the second largest eigenvalue of the hypergraph corresponds to the spectral radius of the graph, following the removal of all edges and certain signed structures.

The impact of Starlink satellites on satellite-based navigation systems like GPS will be substantial, with thousands of Starlink satellites interfering with navigation signals, potentially causing significant degradation in accuracy. To counteract this, a new method called "network coding" has been proposed to mitigate the effects of signal loss and limited visibility. This study investigates the feasibility of using "network coding" to maintain the integrity and accuracy of navigation systems, even under severe interference conditions. It has been found that "network coding" can significantly improve navigation accuracy, with the potential to reduce positioning errors by as much as 66% across a wide range of speeds. Furthermore, "network coding" can also be used to estimate the location of a navigation system even when it is not functioning, providing valuable insights into the effects of signal loss and limited visibility.

The XO-3b planet, a massive hot Jupiter with an unusually high eccentricity of approximately 0.25, orbits an active star that exhibits pronounced variations in its transit timing. Analyzing these timing variations over a period of three years using the TESS and ZTF survey data, we discovered that the fluctuations in the transit times are not only linked to the star's activity but also to the gravitational tidal interactions between the planet and its host star. Our research indicates that the gravitational forces of the star cause the XO-3b's orbit to expand and contract periodically, resulting in variations of approximately 0.5 days in the transit times. Our simulations suggest that the gravitational tidal interactions between the planet and its host, combined with the planet's high eccentricity, are capable of triggering the observed transit timing fluctuations in XO-3b. Our findings have significant implications for the study of hot Jupiters with high eccentricities, as they reveal the potential for tidal interactions to alter the planets' orbits and, in turn, affect the observed transit timing variations.

A new Bayesian calibration approach is developed to accurately determine the parameters of a wave equation describing the behavior of a system over time. The method is applied to a linear one-dimensional wave equation with constant coefficients, where the coefficients are represented by two key parameters, each of which can change randomly. The analysis shows that the posterior distributions of these parameters are distinct, but nearly overlapping, and that the most effective data to analyze is that with high sensitivity and variability. A numerical example is given using a set of simulated data, where the observed system behavior is influenced by a specific event, to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

In this research, we establish a quantitative relationship between moduli space and GW theory of vector bundles on a Richardson-Gieseker bordism class of sheaves on a complex projective manifold, which is based on a previously established quantitative relationship by a different author in a distinct class of sheaves.

We derive novel, consistent prime number theorems for a diverse range of Dirichlet polynomials, generalizing both the original Prime Number Theorem and a generalized form of the logarithmic strong prime number theorem. Furthermore, we establish a generalized version of the Binomial Prime Number Theorem that encompasses the Prime Number Theorem and the binomial variant of the logarithmic strong prime number theorem as special cases. The novel contributions of this note are the inclusion of the binomial case and the derivation of results for exponential Dirichlet polynomials parameterized by arbitrary positive functions.

In modern clinical trials, the traditional randomized design, combining treatment and control groups to test the effectiveness of new treatments, has become increasingly popular with the development of disease-modifying drugs for Alzheimer's disease. However, the unique aspect of treating chronic diseases like Alzheimer's is that the progression of symptoms unfolds over a considerable period, influenced by various factors including age, disease genetics, and lifestyle. Consequently, patients in the control group experience a range of disease progression velocities, resulting in significant variability in their baseline measurements. For example, patients with the APOE4-e4 allele tend to deteriorate faster than their genetically stable peers. Given this variability, employing natural cubic splines to model individual patient trajectories offers a more accurate representation than linear models. Our research leverages this approach in an analysis of disease progression in patients from the Clinical Alzheimer Disease Effects of Rivasomizine Trial, resulting in more precise estimates.

The rapid growth in smart phone usage has led to the development of Crowdsourcing, a technology where individuals can contribute to collective goals through social interaction. However, the current generation of vehicles relies heavily on wired sensors to monitor and report vehicle status, making parking difficult due to the lack of real-time vehicle location feedback. In this research, a novel Crowdsourcing AlgorItmR for WeLcomInG (CRAWLING) is introduced to enhance smart parking systems, enabling vehicles to communicate parking information directly to parking facility managers. This technology, which consists of a wireless sensor node, a control unit, and a parking manager unit, can be integrated into a vehicle's Electronic Control Unit (ECU) for seamless data exchange. Upon vehicle departure, the sensor node is triggered and sends the vehicle location to the control unit, which then sends a command to the parking manager to release the occupied spot. Upon vehicle re-entry, the control unit is triggered, releasing the occupied spot and informing the parking manager via radio. A prototype of CRAWLING was developed and tested in a real-world setting, demonstrating its effectiveness in smart parking systems.

We investigate the behavior of level minimizers, a class of first-order optimization algorithms including gradient descent, Adam, and SGD, when faced with non-convex objectives. It's established that a minimizer of a level conditionally converges to a critical point of the underlying non-convex function, but our research reveals a stronger result: for non-convex functions with a finite level minimum, the minimizer of the level condition actually converges to a global minimum. This knowledge is used to develop a two-stage algorithm, initially searching for a level minimum and then descending from it towards a global minimum. Our approach is grounded in theoretical analysis, yet experiments show that it significantly outperforms conventional methods like Adam and SGD in non-convex optimization tasks.

This paper proposes a novel parametric reflective optical limiter, which offers superior performance characteristics, including extremely low power thresholds ($\mu$Watts) and minimal (sub-dB) attenuation levels. The proposed design is based on a reflective optical power limiter using a single variable width aperture that dynamically adjusts its size in real-time. This compact optical power limiter utilizes an unbalanced Michelson interferometer with a variable beam splitter to control the power output, while an algorithmically controlled (FPGA or DSP) pinhole size is used to set the power threshold and limit the output power to a specific level.

The model incorporates critical aspects of the pandemic, including the severe impact of elderly populations, the significant role of asymptomatic individuals, the high transmission rates of the virus compared to respiratory illnesses, and the substantial reduction in disease transmission resulting from social distancing measures. The model's analytical and numerical solutions reveal that the final outcome depends on the ratio of population ages, infection rates, and social distancing durations. Under certain conditions, particularly when all age groups are exposed, the final outcome is consistently an endemic equilibrium state. The model's predictions show that without acquired immunity, the final outcome is consistently an endemic equilibrium state.
