A collection of infinitely long sequences, each consisting of real numbers with rational endpoints, is considered strongly linked if for every non-empty open set in the space of real numbers (equipped with the lower topology), it contains a subcollection of sequences such that their points are all within the open set. It is also possible to show that any set of sequences that is strongly linked forms a Cantor set in the space of sequences of real numbers, thus being countably compact and closed. However, it's unclear whether such a set of sequences, even if it's closed and countably compact, can be considered strongly linked.

A category $\mathfrak{C}$ of groupoids that includes a certain type of fundamental groupoid $\mathbb{I}(W)$ for a given topological space $W$ is said to have the local uniform property (LUP) if for any map $\eta: X\rightarrow W$ between spaces, there exists a map $\Gamma(\eta): \mathrm{N}(X) \rightarrow \mathrm{N}(W)$ such that for any subset $V$ of $W$, there exists a subset $U$ with $\mathrm{N}(U) = \Gamma(\eta(\mathrm{N}(X)))$. This article explores the Ehresmann semigroups of these groupoids and classifies LUP Ehresmann semigroups based on their Stone spectra. It also studies Ehresmann semigroups with LUP properties and provides a characterization of categories with LUP properties that includes an important theorem on category $\mathfrak{C}$.

The self-focus phenomenon is a well-documented, yet poorly understood, phenomenon of self-amplification observed in various nonlinear systems. This study delves into the relationship between width and depth in self-focus by utilizing a mathematical model to analyze the interaction between width and depth. The results show that the depth of self-focus grows more rapidly than its width as the width increases. This conclusion is supported by numerical simulations of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation in one and two dimensions, establishing the first theoretical connection between width and depth in self-focus. The theoretical connection is also supported by numerical and analytical evidence from the Gross-Pitaevskii model in two dimensions, confirming that the depth grows faster than the width in self-focus.

This research study examines the thermal and viscosities-dependent properties of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles synthesized via a low-temperature technique using a precursor solution. The obtained nanoparticles were characterized by a double-helix structure, double hysteresis loop, and ferromagnetic behavior at room temperature, as evidenced by XRD, XPS, and magnetic measurements. The presence of Fe and Bi elements in the nanoparticles was confirmed by XPS analysis. Furthermore, the optical properties and UV light utilization efficiency of the BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles were also investigated. The nanoparticles were used as a catalyst in hydrogen production and dye degradation, demonstrating their efficacy in both processes, particularly in the degradation of methylene blue dye.

The construction of the ${\rm SU}(6)$ flavor symmetry model for light and heavy pseudoscalar mesons, including those containing charmed, beauty, and strange quarks, is detailed in this study. This ${\rm SU}(6)$ symmetry leads to specific flavor symmetry theorems within the Standard Model, predicting certain outcomes for certain meson decay patterns. Additionally, we identify the impact of the ${\rm SU}(6)$ symmetry on the pseudoscalar meson octet and singlet decay constants, highlighting how their values can be derived using ${\rm SU}(6)$ as well as calculating the decay constants for mesons containing a beauty quark, such as the $\eta_b$ and $\eta_c$. This study also explores the role of the $\tau$ and $b$ quark within the ${\rm SU}(6)$ model, including the prediction for the $\eta_b \to \gamma \gamma^*$ and $\eta_c \to \gamma \gamma^*$ decays, with the former's result being in agreement with the Belle II data.

We introduce an innovative task of generating detailed 3D models of common objects held in hand using only a single image, no 3D model of the object, and only knowledge of its category. Our approach is significant because it can create models that align with real-world shapes, and these models can be used in a variety of real-world applications such as robotic grasping. Our method relies on a deep neural network that generates a mesh representing the object's shape by combining data from hand appearance, point estimates from the scene, and object category. Our approach outperforms previous methods in terms of mesh accuracy and alignment with ground truth shapes, and demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on a common benchmark for hand object recognition. Additionally, we release a new dataset of hand-held objects captured in natural settings, and provide code and data for our method.

The Ca-K index, a crucial solar parameter, has been calculated for 1084 years of data from the Kodaikanal Observatory, with the use of an established formula adjusting the index according to solar activity. This allowed for the creation of a long-term mean series for the Ca-K index and its associated standard deviation, with a linear relationship exhibiting. Analysis of data from the Kodaikanal Observatory revealed a correlation between photospheric magnetic flux, solar radio flux, and the solar wind. Furthermore, a comparison of the long-term mean series with other solar series revealed a significant correlation, with a correlation coefficient of 0.9, in addition to identifying short-term variations in the data.

The Standard Model's simplicity makes it a strong candidate, yet, in the past 60 years, experiments have found subtle anomalies that challenge its basic principles. One notable discrepancy is the notable 3.3 sigma deviation in the branching ratio of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, first observed at the Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) first run, and set by the LHCb collaboration during its second run. This anomaly could be an indication of new physics, particularly of non-standard neutrino interactions (NSNIs) between neutrinos and other particles, as it aligns with predictions from previous studies. In this research, we will reanalyze the data from the LHC's second run using advanced techniques to confirm whether the anomaly is genuine.

A new technique for symbolic analysis is proposed, which is flexible enough to be used in a variety of distributed environments. This method relies on a test-depth segmentation approach that breaks down a non-deterministic program into smaller, more manageable segments. Each segment is analyzed individually, allowing for flexibility in determining the level of distribution. This method is applicable in both centralized and distributed computing settings. Additionally, a proof-of-concept tool has been developed to verify the correctness of test-depth segmentation.

The long-term arrangement of magnetic nanoparticles is a key factor in numerous cutting-edge technologies, encompassing data storage and medical treatments. In this research, we utilize a unique, adaptable framework that combines exact computations with simulations to examine the stable configurations of magnetic nanoparticles in a 2D environment. This model is then applied to investigate the effects of nanoparticle size and proximity to a metal surface on their magnetic ordering patterns. Our study reveals that repulsive forces between the nanoparticles and the substrate significantly influence the arrangement of the particles, leading to a pattern characterized by regular spacing and ordering.

In a collaborative machine learning framework, clients with local data share and collaborate on shared models to leverage this information. However, trusting this data to a central server poses significant security risks, highlighted by recent breaches. To address this, our proposal creates a distributed learning environment free from dependence on a central server. We utilize social network trust properties to combine data from groups of trusted parties. An algorithm, named Distributed Trust Region Covariate Shift, was developed to effectively train models in this framework, demonstrating its superiority over current methods through extensive experiments on various datasets.

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved the performance of natural language processing tasks. This work focuses on developing a comprehensive model for the Brief Text Category (BTC) task, which assigns one of 34 categories to brief text descriptions, given at various input lengths. Our model incorporates recurrent and convolutional neural networks and is tested using the BTC dataset, with results evaluated across two settings: a single, extended input and multiple shorter, individual inputs. Additionally, we propose and evaluate a new metric for the BTC multiple-input scenario.

To analyze the etalons used in spectroscopy with the help of the $F$-function, an analytical expression for telecentric etalons was derived. It takes into account the thickness of the etalon and that of the spacer. This expression is valid for both Fabry-Pérot and Fabry-Pérot-Fano etalons in spatially uniform and spatially non-uniform light conditions. Spatial non-uniformity was accounted for by assuming that the light enters the etalon at an angle. Derivations for the $F$-functions of spatially non-uniform telecentric etalons were provided in a series of papers. Certain limiting cases were also examined, including the influence of the plate's thickness on the etalons and the effect of the plate's thickness on the etalons' performance.

A significant issue in pairing-based cryptography is finding a pairing with desired congraence properties. We introduce congruent pairings, define the criteria for their existence, and develop a method to determine whether a given pairing meets these criteria. Our study reveals that many known pairings exhibit specific congrence properties, while others do not.

To achieve significant cost savings in designing large-scale systems, 3D system-in-package (SiP) configurations are integrating multiple processing and memory functions onto multiple separate die, connected by interdie communication networks. A key challenge in building such configurations is optimizing their architecture to optimize performance, reduce area, and minimize their high and variable costs. This paper proposes using a novel modeling approach, called the Chiplet Cost Model, to help evaluate the economic implications of different design trade-offs for such configurations. This model not only accounts for traditional component costs but also considers the costs associated with integrating chiplets, due to factors like lower yields and increased design times. The paper demonstrates how this model can be used to identify the most cost-efficient design for a given application by optimizing chiplet counts and sizes, and complex interconnect configurations, while taking into consideration both performance and economic factors.

A nonparametric mixture cure model is used to analyze datasets with a non-zero portion of survivors. Estimating the distribution of time until recovery in such datasets is crucial, particularly for high-risk patients. Existing parametric and semiparametric mixture cure models often struggle with nonconvergence due to the intricate nature of the underlying distribution. To address this issue, we introduce a presmoothing method that enhances the assessment of the survival function of time until recovery. Under this approach, the estimated time-to-event variables are initially smoothed and then used for maximum likelihood estimation. We demonstrate the validity of this method through mathematical theorems. Simulation studies confirm its effectiveness in improving the accuracy of recovery rate estimation.

The nonlocal measure dimension, a metric that gauges how effectively a set moves within a space by measuring its elements' influence, is introduced and studied in the context of graphs. This dimension measure serves as an alternative to the classical Assouad dimension and is found to have significant ties to its equivalent, offering a more straightforward and intuitive framework for its analysis. By applying this measure, a novel characterization of Muckenhoupt weight classes is obtained, along with an equivalent definition that relies on nonlocal measure dimension.

In-memory computing is now being leveraged for low-power execution of machine learning algorithms by utilizing in-memory processing engines like oneDyna, which enables the implementation of a single-instruction multiple-data architecture for efficient neural network computations. To evaluate the security of such in-memory processing engines, we developed a security testing framework that allows for large-scale attacks to be performed on a single machine. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our framework by successfully conducting three types of large-scale side-channel attacks that compromise model accuracy: one based on monitoring CPU performance, another based on monitoring network latency, and a more sophisticated attack that utilizes a gradient-based approach to estimate model accuracy. Our results show that even minimal data can be leveraged to significantly decrease model accuracy, with accuracy dropping as low as 26.7% after observing just 10 computations.

This work outlines a method to simplify computational processes in the context of in-medium calculations, primarily applicable to the polarization tensor. The method's effectiveness extends beyond the polarization tensor to other propagators, making it a valuable resource. By reorganizing and restructuring certain terms, we transform the conventional structure of these propagators into a more streamlined framework. This transformation facilitates a more efficient approach to in-medium calculations, both within and outside the soft-external momentum framework.

A novel, non-biased method for reducing seismic noise has been introduced, which utilizes a unique model transfer technique for noise abatement in areas lacking prior seismic data, often occurring in hard-to-reach exploration regions. The new approach employs a pre-trained, generalized model that is not limited by spatial constraints and can effectively apply its noise-reducing capabilities to multiple sites. The model is initially trained on data from areas where noise is not a concern, then fine-tuned for a specific site using data from a secondary, shorter time frame. The model's performance is demonstrated using data from the ETC project, where it effectively mitigated seismic noise in an offshore location by applying the model's noise-reducing capabilities using a 3D convolutional neural network. The new approach has shown to be more efficient and capable of handling complex noise patterns, while also providing a straightforward method for evaluating the model's performance.

The interactions between elastic lepton- and antilepton particles and protons are examined in the context of quantum electrodynamics, with a specific focus on the role of charge asymmetry. By incorporating the charge-asymmetric part of the photon propagator known as the "light-by-light" contribution, we calculate the scattering cross-sections for e- and e+ particles interacting with protons. Our analysis shows that this asymmetry has a noticeable effect on the scattering patterns of e- and e+ particles with both protons.

A recent study utilizing scanning tunneling spectroscopy has investigated the electronic properties of a specific material, Sr$_2$IrO$_4$. The research focused on its behavior at low temperatures, around the Fermi level, and found clear evidence of a gap formation at 0.15 meV. The observed spectrum can be interpreted as a combination of two types of excitations - spin-polarons with certain properties and higher-energy excitations above the gap. The study also revealed that the material exhibits a distinctive, multi-peak structure that is attributed to the lattice vibrations of oxygen atoms near the Fermi level. As light is shined on the material, these peaks transform into a broadened single peak, indicating increased electrical conductivity.

Researchers use mediation analysis to determine whether an intermediate factor influences the relationship between a treatment and an outcome.  In recent years, studies have focused on developing methods that can handle multiple low-influence factors, particularly in situations where these factors are not known.  A new method has been proposed for scenarios involving continuous treatments and binary mediator values.  In this study, we aim to develop and apply a framework for robust causal mediation analysis, allowing for continuous mediator values.  Our approach utilizes a mixed distributional approximation and incorporates a penalty term to handle multiple, unknown influence factors.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using a simulation study and real-world data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, which shows how certain factors, such as body mass index, influence the relationship between smoking and cholesterol levels.  Furthermore, we examine the influence of other factors, like height, diet, and physical activity, on smoking and cholesterol levels.

Over the course of 20 years, the field of starshade technology has undergone significant evolution, with early conceptual studies giving way to more advanced analysis of on-sky deployment and a current focus on a full-scale, operational system. This edition of The Refractor to feature a collection of papers that showcase the latest starlight mimicking systems, as well as a unique historical perspective on the field's development. We take this opportunity to reflect on the progress and challenges faced by the community so far, with a look ahead to the future of exoplanet direct imaging technology. We invite our community to join the discussion and shape the future of starshades.

To effectively combat suicidal behavior, it's crucial to have access to accurate and timely information as quickly as possible. Unfortunately, the online content provided by traditional search engines can be outdated, irrelevant, or misleading, often prioritizing popularity over timeliness. To address this issue, we've created Robin, a comprehensive database of online content related to suicidal behavior that is annotated based on its usefulness and relevance. Our content criteria focuses on resource type, language, and relevance to specific aspects of suicidal behavior such as risk factors and recovery strategies. By utilizing an advanced annotation platform and incorporating international resources, Robin has become the largest and most diverse collection of its kind, encompassing 11 categories and 1,500 annotated documents.

A novel fundamental principle, referred to as Blackian mechanics, is proposed, where the trajectory of any object in a vacuum is determined by the information about the object's surroundings that remains unknown. This concept is exemplified through the simple scenario of a particle traveling in a vacuum where the unknown information influences the speed of the particle proportional to time, leading to an exponential increase in distance traveled over time, represented by the equation $L(t) = \sigma v t$, with $\sigma v$ denoting the uncertainty in velocity.

This research paper explores dynamic characteristics of solutions for a specified difference equation, particularly when subjected to initial conditions that fall within a bounded set. The primary focus lies in determining bounded solutions, and the study employs two methods to achieve this: analytic and numerical analysis. Initially, the research involves the separation of variables to yield bounded solutions for specific $a$ and $\alpha$ values. Subsequently, the study utilizes the Picard's iterative method to derive an iterative formula for an arbitrary initial condition. This formula is utilized to determine bounded solutions for the equation, provided that suitable choices of $a$ are made. The research is complemented by an application of the findings to medical fields, where the study provides new insights into difference equation dynamics.

We develop a group of electrodynamic models based on the Born-Infeld theory, which incorporate non-linear electric and magnetic fields with electric and magnetic dipole and quadrupole moments, both confined within the electrodynamic framework. These non-linear fields are allowed to coexist within the action, which yields a group of theories that expand upon the Maxwell theory. These theories are then applied to a five-dimensional flat space, where charged black holes are found without fine-tuning the parameters. One of these black holes is an exact solution, which includes a specific limit where it becomes a black string-like solution, and another is a thermodynamic phase solution, which depends on the parameters and the properties of the dipole and quadrupole moments, leading to a unique four-dimensional black hole. These black holes are further analyzed using the thermodynamic stability conditions of the black hole.

Consider a linear structure represented by $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ and its associated finite field $F_q$. A set of elements $S$, consisting of $m$ non-zero vectors in $F_q^n$, is classified as a $q^t$-Sidon arrangement if the sum of the products of any two elements from $S$ equals $q^{t-1}$, where the arrangement $S$ is considered for any $t$ value from 1 to $4$. In this study, we delve into the number of $q^2$-Sidon arrangements in $F_q^n$, as well as the number of $q^3$-Sidon arrangements in $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$, provided $q$ is at least 3 and $n$ is at least 4.

The scaling behavior of magnetic susceptibility at finite temperatures has been investigated in the XY model under periodic boundary conditions. This involved calculating magnetic susceptibility due to small external fields applied both parallel and transverse to the spin alignment, as well as the geometric phase, which is associated with the winding number. These calculations, made within the strong coupling expansion, involved an effective mass factor that depends on the external field and the winding number. It was found that the magnetic susceptibility for the XY model shows a power-law dependence on the external field, as well as a power-law dependence on the effective mass factor. Furthermore, the Geometric phase was found to have a dependence on the external magnetic field and the effective mass factor. It was also found that the scaling exponent for the XY model is 3/2, as the critical temperature is proportional to the square of the winding number.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of the Ising model, particularly its transition from a paramagnetic state to either ferromagnetic or spin glass states. Our research focused on understanding the influence of the dynamic exchange coupling on the process, as it's a critical component in modeling materials. The results indicate that, contrary to expectations, the dynamic coupling doesn't have a direct accelerating effect on the transition to ferromagnetism. However, in certain scenarios with short relaxation times, it can promote the formation of short-range ordered domains that facilitate the transition. A detailed analysis of the dynamic behavior revealed a distinct correlation between temperature fluctuations and the process. Our findings suggest that a warmer paramagnetic state actually slows down the transition to ferromagnetism, assuming typical relaxation times remain constant. The results also show that shorter relaxation times can facilitate the transition to ferromagnetism.

In one-dimensional quasicrystals, the motion of particles is restricted to left or right movement within a specific amplitude range, and the probability of movement is determined by a power-law based on the distance between sites. Our research reveals that, for power-exponents less than 1, the motion of particles is localized, resulting in a limited mobility that decreases in proportion to the power-exponent's square root. Conversely, for power-exponents greater than 1, the motion of particles is de-localized, and the probability of movement is determined by a distance power-law that decreases by at least two units. Our findings also show that, for power-exponents greater than 1, the motion of particles is no longer confined to left or right movement within a finite range, and the probability distribution becomes a Gaussian with a mean displacement that increases in proportion to the distance between sites.

Conversational systems that are tailored to a distinct objective are known as task-focused dialog systems. They are widely used in customer service platforms such as virtual travel guides, customer support assistants, and online financial advisors. These systems are typically designed to handle a specific type of user need, and their primary function is to provide accurate task completion while also improving the user experience. 

Developing multilingual task-focused dialog systems is a highly sought-after area of study, and this paper will serve as an introduction to the current state of the art. We will address the essential concepts and challenges in building such systems, and provide a structured review of recent advancements in NLP. We will also explore the limitations of current solutions and propose potential future research directions to further enhance the development of highly accurate and user-friendly task-focused dialog systems.

To gain a deeper understanding of alternative splicing, we analyzed a large dataset from the GENCODE project, which included 1,678 short-term experiments in human cells. We developed a computational method to quantify differential splicing by comparing individual transcripts to those in the GENCODE knowledge base. This approach revealed a vast number of alternative splicing events in individual transcripts, resulting in over 1.5 million novel events. We found that the proportion of alternative splicing events increased with the number of events per gene, which we attributed to a 'building block' mechanism. We also discovered that genes involved in multiple splicing events tend to have high expression levels, which may be related to their diverse functions. Furthermore, we showed that short-term splicing regulation is influenced by gene expression levels, and that the stability of transcripts is influenced by both expression and splicing. Overall, our study suggests that short-term splicing regulation is a complex process that is influenced by gene expression and the stability of transcripts.

A company's data protection policy is essentially a set of guidelines that outline expected behavior when handling personal information. The legal framework that governs data protection is complex, with multiple laws and regulations, including the GDPR and CCPA, and their respective nuances. In light of this, many organizations face a challenge in ensuring their technical teams understand and adhere to these guidelines. To address this issue, we conducted a qualitative study that involved interviewing 11 technical professionals about their experiences with data protection, their understanding of key concepts, and how they applied these principles in their daily work. The results show that this group of participants had varying levels of data protection knowledge, learned through different sources, and often relied on technical strategies to ensure data protection compliance. The participants' knowledge gaps and its consequences, including a perceived disconnect between technical teams and legal/management teams, are also highlighted.

The azimuthal angular correlations between multiple particles produced during proton and ion collisions with other nuclei have been analyzed in a simplified scenario. The analysis considered a single parton interaction and used the Color Glass Condensate effective theory framework. The results showed a significant correlation between the azimuthal angles of charged particles for proton collisions with a lead nucleus at high transverse momenta, and this correlation became less pronounced at lower momenta. For ion-ion collisions, an initial quadrupole pattern developed which was later became circular. The results also showed that even at lower momenta, the correlation between particle azimuthal angles in a specific window was more pronounced in proton and ion collisions with a baryonic nucleus compared to a non-baryonic nucleus like uranium.

The production of light nuclei such as $^{4}$H, $^{4}$He, and $^{3}$H within a simulated collision of gold ions at a energy level of 3 GeV and at midrapidity is analyzed through a coalescence model. This model accounts for the possibility of particles combining in the final state and for the subsequent hadronization of quarks. Calculations are carried out using a model called hadron resonance gas at the partonic stage, and it is found that the coalescence process of particles is influenced by the hadronization process, which leads to a significant reduction in the predicted yields of light nuclei compared to experimental results. Furthermore, this model also fails to capture the observed energy dependence of light nuclei yields due to an overestimation of quark correlations. To address this issue, a new approach called the "correlation-replica approach" is proposed. This model accounts for the correlations of quarks in the late stage of the partonic medium, and it is found to accurately reproduce the experimental data.

The study of exoplanetary science has significantly advanced in recent years, 
thanks to the abundance of exoplanet data that provides valuable insights into 
the properties of planets and their celestial bodies. This knowledge enables us 
to investigate how their environments influence their development, composition, 
formation, and potential for life. This chapter focuses on how certain factors 
such as planetary size, mass, orbital distance, and the type of star they 
orbit around shape the characteristics of rocky planets. We will delve into the 
impact of planetary size and mass on the rockiness of a planet, examine how 
different types of stars affect a planet's temperature and atmospheric retention, 
and explore the effects of a planet's distance from its star on its temperature. 
Lastly, we will discuss the effects of a planet's mass on its development, as well 
as the effects of a planet's orbit on its atmospheric properties.

We investigate the existence of solvable groups whose order equals the chromatic number of specific circulant graphs, utilizing this search for potential applications in designing circulant network topologies that can be configured and managed through polynomial computations.

This paper presents an enhanced iteration method for inverting matrices and introduces an extension to its various forms. It also demonstrates how the extended technique outperforms the traditional methods by reducing the required iterations to find the same level of accuracy, thereby allowing for a faster implementation on graphics processing units. To validate this, we tested the extended iteration methods using the CuBlas library and found they offer a 2-40% improvement in performance compared to the standard CuBlas matrix inversion algorithms for doubly and triply inverted matrices. This performance improvement makes the extended iteration methods suitable for use in the field of control engineering.

We examine the power spectrum of the primordial perturbations in a ultra-slow-roll inflation scenario, taking into account the impact of interactions on perturbations. By employing a slow-roll approximation to calculate the background inflation field dynamics, coupled with a cosmological perturbation theory framework, we derive a linearized equation for the primordial perturbation field. Subsequently, we analyze the equation under slow-roll conditions, solve it using the WKB method, and track the perturbation mode evolution. Our analysis reveals that the power spectrum of the primordial perturbations undergoes a logarithmic divergence during ultra-slow-roll inflation, consistent with findings involving other inflation scenarios.

We've discovered that the common practice of combining multiple selection algorithms to enhance performance does not necessarily lead to superior results.  In our investigation, we explored whether a single optimal selection algorithm exists, and if so, whether it could be more effective than a combination of different algorithms.  To address this query, we defined and analyzed the concept of an optimal single-step selection algorithm, which we referred to as the enhanced selection optimizer (ESO).  We demonstrated that ESO exists for all feasible problem parameters and efficiently computes the optimal solution within polynomial time for certain parameter settings, but this computation becomes impractical for more general parameter configurations.  To overcome this limitation, we introduced a more practical variant of ESO that offers a guaranteed performance improvement over existing methods, and our empirical results confirm the efficacy of this new approach in various real-world applications with diverse parameter settings.

The standard method for reporting survival data involves creating a table using the Kaplan-Meier method, which provides a way to compare groups based on time to an event. However, when there are multiple events with different follow-up times, it's difficult to accurately compare groups. A new method is proposed to address this issue by representing survival data as a series of events over time. This method can be applied to a range of studies, including those that involve counting unique events rather than reporting time-to-event data. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated using a dataset from a breast cancer study that tracked medication use over time. The method is also applied to a study on the effectiveness of the SARS-CoV-2 vaccine in preventing the Omega variant.

High-precision calculations in particle physics necessitate precise numerical evaluation of Feynman integrals.  This requirement has driven advancements in numerical methods for evaluating Feynman integrals over the past few decades.  Although progress has been made in accurately evaluating integrals with diverse loop structures and scale dependencies, complex integrals with many internal propagators and multiple loop loops remain challenging.  In this research, we demonstrate the capabilities of the polyint method for numerical integration of complex Feynman integrals with numerous internal propagators and loop structures.  Through our experiments with various integrals, including up to five-loop examples, we confirm the polyint method's reliability in numerical integration.  Additionally, we verify the polyint method's performance against known results for several benchmark integrals, such as the two-loop master integrals of $\mathcal{V}$.

Modern data storage platforms are expected to integrate both traditional file and grid technologies, offering object-based data retention solutions with improved scalability and performance. To evaluate these systems, our study compares the performance of two platforms, Lustre and DAOS, in terms of object storage operations. The investigation reveals that object-based storage has a substantial impact on file system size in our test scenario. For a file of 1 TB, this size increase amounts to 3.2% (Lustre) to 27% (DAOS) with fixed object storage operations involved. Despite this, object storage operations in both platforms demonstrate comparable execution times, with DAOS taking a notable 0.62% longer time than Lustre. The study further assesses the performance of both platforms in terms of single and multiple client access, showing that DAOS experiences a significant 33% increase in server-side workload. The investigation concludes that object storage operations have a substantial impact on storage efficiency and performance.

A novel system has been proposed to manage electric vehicle charging during peak hours when space is scarce at public parking facilities such as shopping malls, office buildings, and residential areas. The system efficiently allocates limited resources, ensures timely charging sessions for users and operates with minimal computational demands. The system's charging station management module dynamically adjusts the number of available slots based on real-time parking demand and entrance/exits. The system's virtual slot concept allows it to accommodate a large number of users without increasing the physical parking capacity. The virtual slot concept is analogous to a queue, enabling the management module to dispatch and manage the slots. The system's virtual slot management module ensures that the total number of assigned slots does not exceed the physical parking capacity. The efficacy of the system is demonstrated through a simulation-based evaluation that shows its ability to manage and process a substantial volume of users.

This research investigates the presence of linear or quasilinear code classes in the context of linear or quasilinear delta matrices within the framework of finite field theory. It also delves into the creation of linear or quasilinear delta matrix codes and presents several methods for this process.

The quantum gravitational effective action is typically represented by Feynman diagrams with loops containing an arbitrary number of geons, which are elementary objects in classical general relativity. We propose that the classical limit of a loop effectives theory should be characterized by diagrams with two geons only. This approach yields a non-renormalizable action similar to Einstein-Hilbert, and the coefficient of the quadratic divergence aligns with the loop counting of the Feynman diagrams. This finding echoes a similar principle in the 't Hooft loop expansion in Yang-Mills theory.

The transition away from fossil-based power generation is crucial in addressing climate change, but faces obstacles due to high costs and land requirements for renewable energy alternatives. Our study examines the feasibility of decarbonizing the power grid in the Western United States and the land-use implications using either large-scale solar farms or community solar arrays in a multi-regional model. The results show that both solar options can meet the carbon reduction targets under the Clean Power Plan, but differ significantly in their land-use impacts. Community solar arrays come closest to the high capacity of large-scale solar farms at a lower cost, but their land-use efficiency is significantly better. Our findings suggest that a grid-neutral transition to renewable energy can be achieved with minimal land disruption by implementing community solar arrays, thereby overcoming concerns.

Cluster-randomized trials are often employed to estimate treatment effects on binary outcomes by comparing a treatment group and a control group. However, they can also be used to assess treatment effects on population-level effects, such as changes in disease prevalence. Typically, separate estimands are required to account for population-level effects. This study focuses on cluster-randomized trials where treatments are applied at the individual level while randomization occurs at the group level. Estimands are defined to estimate key quantities like the probability of individual-level treatment effects, population-level effects, and the prevalence of a binary outcome within the study population. A comprehensive framework is introduced to conduct inference in these trials, encompassing estimands both at the individual and population levels. This framework considers multiple levels of inference and addresses concerns such as missing data and the risk of type I errors. Its application is demonstrated through an example from a real-world study.

Research on random networks has gained momentum in recent years, with a focus on developing fractal-like networks based on specific network designs. This article explores the analysis of various network measures, such as connectivity, clustering, and energy, for a specific network family known as the Mobius octagonal network. This analysis is conducted under different conditions including regular, random, and percolated scenarios. We also investigate the spectral properties of these networks using the standardized Laplacian spectrum and examine their behavior under different conditions. Furthermore, we create a new variant of the Mobius octagonal network with a 16-arm structure and repeat a similar analysis conducted in the previous one.

We examine a scenario with multiple agents in a distributed system, each facing a sequence of linearly structured tabular bandit problems. The key challenge is for these agents to collaborate without direct access to the global problem matrix. Each agent is given a dataset consisting of a set of linear equations representing relationships between the matrix and observed outcomes. Our proposed distributed algorithm allows the agents to collaborate while only exchanging limited information. The algorithm yields a regret rate equivalent to that of a centralized system, using centralized parameter estimation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm allows the agents to achieve a shared, efficient solution without direct matrix multiplication. The algorithms' performance is supported by empirical, tabular results.

Creating patient datasets with realistic medical histories is crucial for developing and testing healthcare technologies. It's essential for evaluating the effectiveness of new treatments and for conducting ethical analyses. For example, in a study involving a large clinical data set, researchers can determine the anticipated impact of new treatments on the population by comparing past outcomes with historical data. However, accurately replicating real-life patient data in a simulation is often overlooked, resulting in unrealistic outcomes. In this study, a synthetic data approach was used to generate a large, diverse patient dataset of 1.4 million individuals with cystic fibrosis, allowing for a detailed comparison of synthetic records with actual patient data. The data indicates that the synthetic population is more diverse than the real one in terms of age, sex, and ethnic distribution. The $X(3872)$ is found at 3818.3 MeV with a total width of 2.16 MeV, a total width of 1.3 MeV, a branching fraction of 2.51 $\pm$ 0.20 $\pm$ 0.13 $\pm$ 0.3 $\pm$ 0.3 $\%$ and a decay angle distribution consistent with a molecular interpretation. This research introduces a new computational method for assessing the originality and disruptiveness of bibliometric and patent data, specifically designed for evaluating the value of scientific publications, technologies, and innovations. By analyzing citation networks, this approach generates quantitative representations of publications and their corresponding connections. It calculates various metrics to quantify the originality and disruptiveness of each publication, which can be refined and combined as needed. These metrics are further categorized into three groups: measurement, modeling, and analysis. Our method is implemented in a Python library called Novelpy, which is freely available for use in research and development.

To study the effects of cross-phase modulation, we have analyzed the interaction between two light beams in a nonlinear medium. We found a solution for the coupled equations governing this interaction, and our results show that introducing a temporal gradient to the controlling beam creates a corresponding gradient in the controlled beam. This effect allows for the dynamic control of many properties, such as the controlled beam's pulse duration, carrier envelope frequency, amplitude, and chirp. Additionally, we demonstrate that spatial and temporal modulation techniques can be combined to produce a wide range of adjustable output beams.

Human performance in specific tasks often cannot be improved upon by current artificial intelligence (AI) systems. This research explores the ability of contemporary machine learning models to replicate the expertise of an Olympic-level archer in evaluating the technical aspects of a bowstring. Building upon previous research that demonstrated the inability of AI to match human expertise in certain areas, our findings indicate that a well-trained model can indeed reach the level of expertise required to participate in a world archery competition. However, further investigation suggests that a model must acquire the benefits of personalized practice with a specific bowling machine in order to reach that level.

In cross-domain recommendation, we're tasked with identifying items that are likely to be appealing to users across multiple platforms, despite having limited information available on those users. One of the primary challenges is that we often lack the specific information needed to gauge a user's interest in a particular item on a target domain, making it difficult to make informed recommendations. To address this issue, we're proposing a dual-metric approach that enables our model to develop a deeper understanding of user preferences in the target domain. By leveraging this knowledge, our model can make more effective recommendations on the target domain, even when limited information is available. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by testing it on two real-world datasets with cross-domain recommendation tasks, resulting in superior performance over existing models. A closer examination of our model's behavior reveals that it learns to capture user preferences in the target domain, effectively improving recommendations on that domain. Furthermore, we're able to enhance our model's performance by incorporating knowledge graph embeddings, effectively transferring user and item representations across platforms.

We present a characterization for a specific fragment of the $\mu$-calculus, known as $\mu$SEG, by linking it with a particular kind of logical expressions, called $\mu$-formulas, on the basis of an efficient model-theoretic interpretation. This fragment includes the $\mu$CAL fragment, commonly used in decentralized systems. We expand on the existing characterization by showing that our proposed approach supports modular refinement, known as Hennessy-Milner games and tests, enabling the decidability of equivalence assessment for $\mu$SEG. This is achieved through the use of an efficient model-theoretic interpretation on the basis of an abstract, unlabeled, and infinite state space.

This paper explores thermal convection in the context of a two-dimensional, intricately shaped plasma chamber. The shape of the layer, determined by a series of interconnected arcs, is defined by a mathematical formula. The outer boundary of the chamber is assumed to be rigid and insulated, while the inner boundary is maintained at a constant temperature. The temperature patterns within the chamber are investigated through direct numerical simulations, spanning a range of Rayleigh and Prandtl numbers. The findings reveal that the shape of the chamber significantly influences the characteristics of the thermal plumes. In particular, it is observed that an increase in the number of arcs leads to a reduction in plume size and maximum temperature. Furthermore, it is found that plume behavior is non-dimensionalized by a new Rayleigh number, derived from the characteristic length scale of the plenary section and the layer's thickness. The results also indicate that maximum temperature and plume size are accurately predicted by scaling laws based on the Rayleigh number, the number of arcs, and the characteristic length scale.

The goal of supervised classification is achieved by identifying the membership of a test vector to a particular class among multiple available options. This is done by comparing the test vector to a set of labeled training vectors, each corresponding to a class. However, in certain scenarios, the available training vectors are incomplete or non-linearly transformed from the actual classes, resulting in a challenge for the supervised classification task. This paper addresses the problem by leveraging the concept of linear mixtures in an attempt to recover the original classes. Using the principles of sparse optimization, the paper presents an algorithm capable of accurately reconstructing the original classes when their representative vectors are linearly combined with minimal levels of noise. This algorithm is substantiated by both numerical simulations and an experimental validation on image data derived from the CIFAR-10 dataset.

The use of deep learning to reduce X-ray radiation in cardio-angiography is explored through video interpolation techniques. By leveraging the temporal redundancy of these applications, it's possible to decrease the X-ray exposure by adopting a 'capture, predict and continue' approach. This involves capturing an initial frame, predicting the subsequent frame using a deep neural network, and then obtaining the final image through superposition. By limiting the number of X-ray exposures, it's possible to decrease the total dose of radiation emitted during cardio-angiography procedures.

Research on heavy-flavor physics at high-energy $e^+e^-$ colliders is rapidly expanding, driven by advancements in both theoretical modeling and experimental observation. Recent studies at BESIII and Belle-II have found discrepancies in semi-leptonic $B$-meson decays from Standard Model predictions, sparking a need for further investigation. This contribution to the 2021 FCC-ee Community Report assesses the feasibility of measuring heavy-flavor production cross sections at the FCC-ee using the FLFLA2 and PHOTOS events, exploring how precision and detector design intersect in this context. Findings suggest that the FCC-ee could provide the first-ever measurements of inclusive non-relativistic quantum chromodynamics (NRQCD) cross sections for $B_c$ and $B$ mesons produced through double-bottomonium states. Furthermore, by studying the interdependence of detector design and heavy-flavor physics, researchers can optimize detector resolution functions for heavy quarks and improve the accuracy of measuring semi-leptonic $B$-meson decay rates at Belle-II.

In extended theories that incorporate Standard Model gauge symmetries, novel doublet fermions can form to achieve a few notable outcomes, such as a brief neutrino lifetime and the suppression of $\mu \to e \gamma$ and $\mu \to e \gamma \gamma$ decays. A specific low-energy effective theory reveals that a particular neutrino model, $U(1)_{L_e-L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}$, can satisfy the requirements for both the leptophilic $U(1)$ model and the suppression of $\mu \to e \gamma \gamma \gamma$ decay. This model, however, contradicts the predicted neutrino lifetime and presents an intriguing alteration.

The dynamical evolution of stellar populations within the Galactic center is significantly influenced by stellar collisions and the ejection of high-speed stars due to strong gravitational forces. This research investigates the effect of a long-term perturbation on the dynamics of a binary system consisting of a massive star and an intermediate-mass partner. The results show that the long-term orbital evolution leads to a high eccentricity and pericentric passage of the massive star, causing a close encounter that ejects the intermediate-mass partner from the system at velocities exceeding 500 km/s. The study provides a theoretical explanation for the origin of hypervelocity stars and offers a new perspective on the role of secular perturbations in shaping the dynamics of the Galactic center.

This paper examines a specific class of multiplicative stochastic differential equations driven by Brownian motion on a complete probability space, which exhibits singular behavior at zero due to the linear drift at that point. We show that for any equation that is locally Lipschitz elsewhere and singularly multiplicative at zero, the solution's existence is guaranteed, and the solution maps map feeble (cadlag right-continuous with left-bound CADLag values) functions to the same upon weak modifications. We achieve this by applying a novel method of perturbing the equation through the addition of a non-zero, CADLag, and bounded 'disturbance' term, which is then removed in the limit. Consequently, the existence of lower semi-continuous solutions is also established.

We've developed a new method to study properties of $\omega_1$, by using specific mathematical structures $L_0$, and proving that the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ is definable under certain conditions, $T_0$, and its associated theory is consistent with $L_0$. This is achieved without relying on PFA or the existence of a closed unsplit tree. The nonexistence of a continuous increasing continuous surjection $f$ from $\omega_1$ to $\omega_1$ is also an outcome of our method, which has further applications in other contexts.

Achieving top-tier performance in NLP tasks often requires substantial fine-tuning of large language models, a resource-intensive process. Recently proposed adapter methods have shown promise in significantly reducing the computational burden by fine-tuning only the adapter layer of a pre-trained language model, thus allowing the model to learn task-specific knowledge. However, current adapter approaches are primarily based on embedding adjustments, neglecting the potential for the model to acquire task-specific information through changes in output layer properties. We introduce a novel hybrid adapter framework that leverages goal-oriented adaptations, encompassing both embedding and output layer adjustments to facilitate knowledge transfer between pre-trained and task-specific models. We demonstrate that this framework effectively facilitates efficient knowledge transfer and outperforms embedding-focused methods, especially when applied to complex tasks.

The domain of Computer Vision has seen a significant upsurge in interest, primarily due to the potential for automated data analysis, which can significantly reduce the workload of professionals. In this paper, the process of utilizing Computer Vision algorithms for traffic sign detection and categorization is examined. Given the importance of traffic signs in ensuring public safety, the development of efficient algorithms for this task is a critical area of research. However, the lack of annotated data for non-developed countries poses a significant challenge for identifying and categorizing traffic signs in these regions. To address this issue, the Mapillary Traffic Sign Dataset has been created, which offers a diverse range of images from non-developed countries. This dataset contains 1,760 images, each containing numerous traffic signs, which have been annotated with bounding boxes and categorization. We have also introduced a novel evaluation metric known as the Recognition@N score, which measures the accuracy of categorizing traffic signs. We have evaluated various algorithms, including a simple template-based approach and a deep learning-based model, which outperformed the baseline templates with a significantly higher Recognition@N score.

Traditional collaborative filtering techniques struggle to handle data sparsity and diversity issues, and recent self-supervised methods have emerged as an alternative. These self-supervised techniques utilize additional unlabeled data to train proxy models, but they often neglect the interaction between users and users or items, and they lack the ability to utilize labeled data for improved performance. To address these limitations, we propose SelfCF, a novel self-supervised cooperative filtering framework that incorporates two proxy networks for improved performance. SelfCF incorporates a proxy network for user-item interaction and another for user-cohesion, and it leverages a novel contrastive loss function to enhance the proxy networks' representation capabilities. Furthermore, SelfCF seamlessly integrates supervised learning into self-supervised training, and it incorporates a user clustering module to simulate real-world data diversity. Experimental results demonstrate that SelfCF surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets by a significant margin.

We establish that the second homotopy group of projective space of dimension one, denoted as $\mathbb{P}^1$, is isomorphic to the direct sum of integers, and utilize this group to classify projective morphisms from a scheme to projective space of dimension one. Furthermore, we utilize these classifications to derive generalizations of the so-called 'Tevelev inequalities'.

A novel two-dimensional system has been proposed, featuring an insulating structure with unique parabolic and linear dispersive properties. This system, characterized by specific parabolic and linear terms in its effective Hamiltonian, hosts Dirac-like fermions within the system's gap. The system's band structure can be precisely tailored by adjusting its parameters, ultimately yielding a topological phase transition at a specified parabolic-linear coupling threshold. The research demonstrates that this system can be created in two-dimensional tunneling graphene systems, comprised of a trilayer structure with opposing potential barriers.

A fundamental limit in the accuracy of measurements comes from the accuracy of our current understanding of the Universe's initial state. The detection of non-standard cosmological phenomena, such as non-linear dynamics, offers a means to surpass this limitation. The detection of gravitational waves provides a unique opportunity to investigate non-standard dynamics, and this work focuses on elevated modes of gravitational waves that can serve as indicators of the Universe's initial conditions. We propose a method for the detection of these elevated modes in the tritium era of cosmology, a period characterized by significant energy contributions from regular matter, dark matter, and a scalar field. The tritium era takes place when the Universe's age is around 10 billion years. We calculate the amplitude of these elevated modes and determine the sensitivity of future gravitational wave detectors, including a space-based detector, and a ground-based detector, the Einstein Telescope. The findings indicate that these detectors may be capable of detecting these elevated modes, and our research suggests that they could offer a means to surpass the current limit on cosmological precision measurements.

Astronomers have long sought to derive precise orbits for binary star systems.  Recent breakthroughs in astrometry from space-based observations such as Gaia have greatly enhanced the ability to identify and measure binary star systems.  Specifically, its astrometric precision has enabled the measurement of orbital semimajor axes that are measured in milliarcseconds, equivalent to a precision in angular mass of 10^-8 solar masses.  This paper aims to investigate the effectiveness of using parallax measurements from Gaia in determining binary star systems with wide orbits.  It begins by examining the impact of parallax errors on mass estimates and then models the probability distribution of these errors.  The study also investigates the influence of parallax errors on mass estimates and identifies a threshold below which orbital solutions can be confidently determined.  The analysis reveals that parallax errors have the most significant impact on binary systems with large parallax errors and large semimajor axis ratios.  The study provides a comprehensive assessment of the orbital solution reliability for binary star systems with large semimajor axis ratios.  The data from the Gaia Early Data Release 3 is then examined to determine the orbital solution reliability for a large sample of binary star systems.  The results indicate that nearly 60% of the binary star systems have orbital solutions that can be confidently determined.  The study also finds that the orbital solution reliability is heavily influenced by parallax errors, orbital solutions with large parallax errors are more likely to be unreliable.

The 0/1 Knapsack Problem holds significant real-world significance, prompting the exploration of multiple algorithms to address it. Genetic Allocations, a genetic algorithm specifically designed for NP-complete problems, incorporates a unique representation and mutation technique to address these issues. In this study, we examine the effectiveness of various crossover and selection techniques with the Genetic Allocations algorithm when applied to three notoriously challenging NP-complete problems, namely the 0/1 Knapsack, Travelling Salesman, and 0/1 Unweighted Vertex Cover Problems.

This article is focused on the $L^2$-boundedness of trilinear oscillatory integrals defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$, specifically with respect to the parameters $\tau, \lambda, \mu$, and $h$. These oscillatory integrals take the form $\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{i(\tau(x_1-x_2)\tau t_1 + i\lambda(x_1^2-t_1^2)h + i\mu(x_2^2-t_2^2)h}f(x_1,t_1,x_2,t_2)(t_1,t_2) h}$ and involve a smooth function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with smooth estimates. The article establishes that the operator $T_{\tau,\lambda,\mu,h, f}$ is bounded on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$, with specific estimates of the norm depending on the parameters $\tau, \lambda, \mu$, and $h$.

Discriminatory speech has become a pressing global issue, necessitating a comprehensive approach that incorporates artificial intelligence, language filtering, and human intervention. A new dataset, HATRED, is introduced to support the development of a model that identifies and counteracts hate speech. This model, built on the T5 architecture, is trained using an enriched version of HATRED, which yields superior results compared to other models. Notably, the model's performance on hate detection enters a phase of diminishing returns, underscoring the limitations and potential risks of relying solely on AI in addressing hatred. To this end, human involvement is emphasized as an indispensable component in the detection and mitigation of hate speech.

We're examining how to accurately calculate the interactions within complex systems using Quantum Monte Carlo methods. Currently, solving the many-body problem is hindered by the difficulty of calculating the two-body interaction potential, particularly when dealing with systems containing ions with high nuclear charges. Our approach involves breaking down the two-body interaction into two components: the non-relativistic quantum interaction and the relativistic, but non-quantum, interaction. By doing so, we can improve computational efficiency. Furthermore, we're studying the scaling properties of these interactions within Quantum Monte Carlo methods using highly advanced methods, such as the Diffusion Monte Carlo with Jastrow Correlations. Our results show that the complexity of calculating these interactions is directly proportional to the number of particles and the squared nuclear charge. However, incorporating relativistic effects into the interaction introduces an additional level of complexity. Our findings suggest that, in order to efficiently calculate interactions within systems containing ions with high nuclear charges, we must either develop more efficient computational methods or more precise mathematical techniques for resolving complex many-body problems.

The 2020 US General Election raised concerns about election integrity, with false claims about voting systems spreading rapidly through social media. Antidote to Disinformation (AD) projects aim to counteract the effects of misinformation, requiring datasets like VoterFraud2020 to study the spread of misleading information online. Created in partnership with the Stanford Digital Human Insights Initiative (DHII), this dataset comprises 4.5 million tweets (from September 2020 to January 2021) linking to or referencing voting systems, election officials, or election-related entities. Each tweet is annotated with detailed metadata, including labeled misinformation (about voting systems, election officials, or results), accompanied by specific topic labels and false information types. Additionally, a sophisticated search function and API are available for efficient data retrieval. Researchers used this dataset to identify and categorize misleading claims and assess the effectiveness of counter-narratives in the discussion of the US Election, discovering that false claims about voting systems and election officials were the most prevalent types of misinformation examined.

For a subset of $m+1$ holomorphic functions, $P(z)$ and $Q_{1},\ldots, Q_m$ with $Q_1$ nonconstant, we create polynomials $P_{\epsilon}$ and $Q_{\epsilon}$ that deviate from $P$ and the sums $P+Q$ and the sums of $Q_1$ and $Q$ respectively, with a small positive value $\epsilon$. It's proven that for a neighborhood around the $m+1$ zeros of $Q$, there exists a new neighborhood around the $2m+1$ zeros of $Q_{\epsilon}$ where, under a specified condition, the dynamical system formed by $P_{\epsilon}$ and $Q_{\epsilon}$ exhibits certain Lyapunov exponents and normal hyperbolicity properties, similar to those seen in the dynamical system formed by $P$ and $Q$ at a generic point. This result expands upon existing work, allowing for a more general class of maps, including non-orientation preserving ones, and a broader scope of Lyapunov exponents values.

This research introduces a novel approach called encoding, which extracts the posterior distribution's essential information from Bayesian Neural Networks and utilizes it to estimate uncertainty, resulting in improved performance comparable to MCMC techniques. By incorporating encoding, we developed a method referred to as 'encoding' uncertainty measurement, which outperformed the current state-of-the-art solution, 'variance filtering,' in both the prediction and uncertainty calculation aspects, as evidenced by higher accuracy and larger calibration intervals. Furthermore, we developed a 'hybrid' method that combines variance filtering and encoding, leading to a superior uncertainty estimation model with minimal additional costs. The 'hybrid' method yielded the highest accuracy and calibration interval. All associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/lyqhyu/encoding-uncertainty.

The concept of tunneling double-sided imaginary time trajectories in a Euclidean path integral is examined for its potential to simplify quantum particle tunneling calculations. This approach is particularly useful in describing electron transfer processes, as it offers a more detailed understanding of the rate at which they occur. This approach is analogous to the Marcus Levich Jortner (MLJ) theory of non-adiabatic electron transfer, where the rate is influenced by the overlap of wave functions at the reaction site. However, the MLJ theory does not account for variations in temperature or solvent fluctuations. By incorporating the influence of path-weighted fluctuations along with the reaction coordinate, the MLJ theory can be extended to account for these variations. This approach is exemplified through a simple two-dimensional harmonic potential system.

In the context of managing complex pathways in a supply chain, network design plays a vital role. A network design issue can be broken down into three distinct components: (1) a set of potential nodes that need to be considered; (2) a set of feasible routes between these nodes; and (3) a set of decision variables representing the capacity of each route. However, traditional approaches to network design typically focus on either identifying the optimal set of nodes or finding the capacity values for pre-defined pathways, but not on simultaneously optimizing both in a way that is suitable for large-scale problems. To address this limitation, a novel hybrid approach is proposed. This approach combines a heuristic algorithm with a classic integer programming method to find the optimal set of nodes and the capacity values for pre-defined pathways. In a test scenario involving a set of randomly generated networks, the proposed approach outperforms existing algorithms, particularly when the number of nodes is large and the capacity values are not the primary focus.

A theoretical investigation into the thermoelectric properties of Fe$_3$Si thin films has been conducted. Experimental data show that Fe$_3$Si exhibits an exceptionally large thermopower response when its thickness is in the range of 20-40 nm. A proposed thermoelectric drag mechanism has been developed to explain this phenomenon, and this concept has been incorporated into a previously established theoretical framework. This framework provides a detailed theoretical understanding of the thermoelectric behavior of thin films, taking into account both the drag effect and the contributions from charge and thermal carriers. Using this model, it has been predicted that Fe$_3$Si films exhibit excellent thermoelectric properties, including a high thermopower value of over 500 microVolts per degree and a high power conversion efficiency of up to 20 percent. These predictions are in line with experimental findings and indicate that Fe$_3$Si films possess potential as a thermoelectric material.

The Ideal sum problem, a fundamental challenge in number theory, has garnered significant attention, with notable efforts devoted to solving it efficiently. Notably, in 2011, Bostan et al. developed an algorithm that can resolve the problem in $L(1+\epsilon)$ time, but with a substantial limitation: it can only yield a solution that is off by a factor of $2^{\epsilon}$. Our research builds upon this breakthrough, offering a stochastic approach that can produce solutions with more precise estimates while maintaining the same runtime complexity, and in addition, our algorithm runs in the same amount of time as the previous one.

This paper presents an in-depth examination of the irreducible polynomials of specified degrees in a finite field, specifically $\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$, where $k$ is an integer greater than 2. The focus lies in two types of polynomials: those defined by binomials and their constituent minimal polynomials. The study reveals a comprehensive, explicit description of these polynomials' factors and their relationships to specific subsets within $\mathbb{Z}/(kT)$, where $T$ is a prime number with certain conditions, specific to $k$. Furthermore, this research provides a detailed understanding of the properties of minimal polynomials and their explicit expressions, specifically for $k=4$. The findings also uncover patterns in the distribution of irreducible polynomials within specific groups and establish connections between these polynomials and specific subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/(kT)$.

In recent years, formal methods have gained significant importance in software development due to their ability to ensure the correctness of the software. This paper introduces a paper where we have incorporated the UPPAAL tool to facilitate an in-depth examination of source code. Our approach is divided into three distinct stages, which are heavily reliant on UPPAAL's capabilities. Initially, we utilize UPPAAL to generate a temporal formula from the source code. This is followed by an evaluation of the sample input to verify whether it satisfies the formulated formula. Finally, a set of samples is constructed, which are then analyzed using UPPAAL to ensure they conform to the specified properties. This paper presents the results of our initial experiment, which focuses on examining the sample inputs from the well-known Linux operating system.

We investigate the use of metasurfaces for compressive imaging, where a programmable surface is placed behind an object and shines light onto a 2D detector, such as a CCD or CMOS sensor, to capture an image. This setup, where light is directly directed to the sensor without a lens, allows for the capture of a larger field of view in a single image, but introduces a non-linear relationship between the object and the captured pixels. Our work focuses on developing a metasurface that can correct for this non-linearity by studying the spectral reflectivity patterns of the surface. By analyzing the phase profiles of the surface, we are able to reconstruct the spectrum of the surface's response to the object. Our approach is end-to-end, meaning we can start with a 2D image of the object and directly retrieve the spectrum of the surface's response. Our findings show that the best results are achieved when the surface's response is a Hadamard matrix, allowing for the direct reconstruction of the object's spectrum using the Hadamard transform.

In a recent study, the theoretical concept of "ac-shifted" frequencies was introduced through both semi-classical and adiabatic perturbation theories in the context of two-photon transitions in atoms exposed to bichromatically circularly polarized laser fields. This study now confirms these findings experimentally by examining two-photon transitions in Rb atoms between the $10D_{3/2}$ and $11P_{3/2}$ states. Notably, the observed two-photon frequency upshifts were found to be in agreement with the predicted values from both theoretical approaches.

The combination of images from two different sources produces a new image known as an image blend. This paper explores the visualization of a data set by mapping class labels to image blends. The goal is to make the class labels of an unknown image determinable by analyzing the resulting image blends with the data set's images. To achieve this, we introduce a technique that flips the meanings of image class labels by modifying the color palettes of images based on their respective labels. This color-based transformation is referred to as semantic swapping. By applying this transformation to training images and using a Generative Adversarial Network, we create a model that can generate blended images when given an unknown image's class labels. The accuracy of this model is evaluated by checking if the resulting image blends contain both original class labels and the unknown image's label. The results show that using semantic swapping significantly enhances the model's accuracy.

Gene expression can be viewed as a complex, multi-state system that makes transitions according to a probability schedule determined by its environment. To better understand this process, researchers study the path a multi-state system traverses over time. Although this approach is useful, the resulting data is often difficult to interpret directly. In response to this challenge, we have developed a method for extracting insights from the trajectory data that reveal how environmental conditions affect gene expression. Our method can be utilized to determine whether a particular environmental change has any effect, the speed at which a change occurs when there is one, and the timeframes during which a particular change has the most significant impact. Additionally, we have developed a way to use this method on a large set of trajectory data to identify which parts of the path are most informative for answering specific questions about the system.

In the field of education, there's a growing need to understand how technology affects student outcomes and what role it should play in educational settings. To address this, we're providing access to a dataset offering insights into how technology use influences diversity-related outcomes for over 36,000 students across 72 institutions. By leveraging this data, researchers can answer questions about the effectiveness of educational interventions, the impact of technology, and the relationship between diversity metrics. Our goal is to support a broader conversation about the role of technology in education by making this data available. We are also developing a new, more effective model that relies on both educational and non-academic data, and aim to give educators the tools they need to measure the impact of various educational approaches.

A widely employed strategy for solving complex optimization problems via quantum computing involves layerwise quantum approximate optimization, where each layer is optimized separately before being combined into a single circuit. This method has been used to solve problems on quantum devices like the IBMQ system. However, our research reveals a potential issue with this approach, specifically that the quantum circuit design leads to a phenomenon known as overloading in quantum circuits. This issue arises when the amplitude of states in subsequent layers becomes too large, causing the circuit to malfunction. Our findings indicate that overloading can occur in quantum circuits used for layerwise quantum approximate optimization and negatively impact their performance. To demonstrate this issue, we tested a quantum hybrid algorithm on the IBMQ system and observed its decline in performance due to overloading. Our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding overloading in quantum circuits and offers potential solutions to mitigate its impact.

The human identification system, which is essential for our daily lives, has significant implications for our personal liberty.  The ability to unambiguously identify an individual, which is often referred to as re-identification, has substantial consequences for our privacy.  In this study, we examine the level of unambiguity in re-identifying individuals within a dataset, which is a critical issue in evaluating the privacy risks associated with data releases.  We introduce a set of measures that quantify the degree of uncertainty in re-identifying individuals within a dataset, and we also develop methods to estimate these metrics accurately from pre-processed data.  We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed methods on a range of data types, including both controlled data generated for testing purposes and genuine medical data from a hospital setting, and our results demonstrate the practical applicability of these measures in assessing data releases for human re-identification risks.

The increasing availability of fine-grained data from smart meters and IoT devices in recent years has significantly enhanced the detail and accuracy of time series data for electricity consumption. This research paper leverages this information to restore missing time series data based on pre-existing knowledge derived from historical consumption patterns of individual appliances. A data-driven approach is proposed, comprising four key components: a pre-processing stage, a module for learning appliance characteristics, a module for generating templates, and a module for high-resolution recovery. This approach was tested using 2,588 households from California, quantifying the impact of different weather conditions and the effects of shifts in consumer behavior over time.

We examine a modified version of the proximal algorithm, where the crucial component is replaced by a strongly monotone operator, and demonstrate that this augmented algorithm remains convergent. Furthermore, we establish that its sequence of solutions converges to the sole solution of the associated variational inequity problem. Additionally, the consistency of this solution can be verified through the strict feasibility of the solution set. To validate our claims, numerical examples illustrating algorithmic stability are presented in appendices.
