Analysis of the spectra revealed a similar 1-2 second timescale for the two flares, while line intensity ratios varied between 2-4. The 1401-1402 angstrom line showed a more pronounced correlation with He II emission lines, suggesting it is more sensitive to electron beam interactions with the chromosphere. The 1398-1401 angstrom line showed a stronger correlation with H-alpha emission lines, indicating its increased sensitivity to the low chromosphere. The 1401-1402 angstrom line showed a more intense response to flare onset, while the 1398-1401 angstrom line showed a more intense response to flare offset. The rapid transition times between the two Si IV lines, within 1-2 seconds, are consistent with the timescales of the H-alpha and He II emission lines.

We investigate the axion's fate, particularly its potential conversion from a light pseudoscalar meson to a universal ultraviolet (UV) particle. A general theorem reveals that if an axion remains stable at a relatively low energy level, it must be an UV particle. Based on this concept, we demonstrate that the QCD axion is unlikely to be the only viable candidate. A novel characteristic of the UV axion is its ability to exhibit both P and CP symmetry breakings simultaneously. A unique property of the light axion is that it can be transformed into a universal UV particle, eliminating the need for additional assumptions. We also examine the potential of the light axion to be transformed into a universal UV particle, finding that its occurrence is contingent on the presence of a specific energy scale. A notable example is the process by which the CP dilemma axion is converted into a universal UV particle, requiring an energy scale exceeding 100 TeV. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the electric dipole moment of the up quark and the potential for the QCD axion to be transformed into a universal UV particle, finding that a value of $d_u\gtrsim 7.9\cdot 10^{-20}\,{\rm cm}$ would result in its conversion.

The impact of individual physical processes on the critical angle for thin, irradiated semiconductor surfaces is analyzed using Monte Carlo simulations. Specifically, we investigate the effect of applying stopping power tables versus free electron model approximations, as well as the influence of simulations with and without energy loss considerations. Our results show that using free electron model approximations reduce the critical angle by decreasing the range of self-absorbed layers and enhance the agreement with experimental RBS data. In addition, simulations without energy loss considerations yield a better correlation with RBS data for thicker membranes, whereas for thinner membranes, simulations with energy loss predictions provide superior correlation.

The source code verification approach, analogous to physical checks for stolen goods, employs a modified, unrecognizable code code name to verify authenticity, much like physical checks for stolen goods. Verifying digital information in its final form is a fundamental challenge. A method for digital execution exists, commonly referred to as virtual execution. This method enables the running of an original program without altering its syntax. This paper introduces a novel approach to source code execution, utilizing the routing method, which transforms source code into an abstract, unrecognizable code name before running it. A crucial feature of this method is its ability to transform source code syntax, replacing key words with interchangeable alternatives. A study was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of this method in identifying plagiarism, utilizing a test subject written in C#. The test subject's compiled code is encoded using the AES algorithm, and a comparison was made between the original and encoded code. The results revealed a 93% success rate in reconstructing the original code, and a test of the routing method was performed using a C# compiler. The test was conducted on a test subject containing loops, variables, and conditional statements, and a compiled executable was created. Running the encoded test subject in a Windows environment produced identical results to running the original C# compiler, and a comparison was made with existing virtual execution technologies. The experiment demonstrated a 93% success rate in reconstructing the original source code, and a benchmarking test showed the encoded code to be 1.78 times larger

The asymptotic behavior of an automorphic function along a specific matrix is examined within a group of diagonal 2x2 matrices, resulting in an extension of a known result by Hoffmann from 1959. The proof of a specific conjecture by Selberg, concerning the complete convergence of a family of Dirichlet sums, is established under certain conditions governing the cusp shapes.

We investigate the properties of groups that act isometrically on Riemannian manifolds with specific boundary features. Under the assumption that such a group features metric near-subgroups, we establish that it is commensurable with the group consisting of translations within Euclidean space. Additionally, we present an example to demonstrate that this condition does not necessarily imply the group's finiteness.

We introduce a new approach to calculate the likelihood of a log-concave probability density function based on randomly selected samples. Our method bypasses the time-consuming task of calculating log-concave density estimates, instead utilizing a sequence of simpler linear programming problems to derive a series of progressively more accurate probability estimates. These estimates can be combined to approximate the likelihood of a log-concave log-density estimate, obtained through a sequence of linear programs that are straightforward to solve. The proposed method can generate samples from the estimated density by solving a linear programming problem and then selecting a random portion of the resulting result. Our theoretical findings demonstrate that the accuracy of these estimations and samples improves at a near-exponential rate, and also demonstrate the practical utility of our approach. The theoretical results were validated through numerical simulations, in which our approach demonstrated significantly improved accuracy compared to other methods. The real-world effectiveness of our approach was also validated by its application in a speech recognition task, in which it produced results comparable to or superior to those achieved by other methods.

Researchers have employed the Wang-Landou algorithm to calculate the entropy of systems in equilibrium by sampling microstates. We have adapted this algorithm to calculate the entropy of static granular assemblies by simulating the static configuration of the grains in a volume-based framework. To achieve this, we have developed a method to identify unique microstates with equivalent volume and minimal overlap, and used this approach to investigate the relationship between disorder and entropy in granular assemblies. Our findings show that the entropy of random packings is significantly influenced by their volume and packing efficiency, and we have also identified a unique relationship between disorder and entropy in packings of disordered spheres.

We explore an adapted version of an earlier game called Adventurer-Manager in a network structure known as a graph. In this modified version, two players make moves sequentially, taking turns to execute specific actions. The first player's moves involve either advancing the Adventurer across certain connections or staying still, while the second player's moves involve either staying still or making the Manager move with a designated node. The overall goal is for the Adventurer to reach a specific destination node without certain connections being formed, or the Manager is allowed to make specified moves. We have established the solvability criteria for networks of a specific structure in relation to different strategies used by the Manager, and also determined the minimum and maximum number of moves required to achieve this goal.

The spectral distribution of a Gaussian process in a single trajectory has distinct frequency-frequency relationships that can be visualized through a coherence function. This article investigates and mathematically defines this coherence function in both time and space domains, revealing its unique properties and similarities to classical random frequency spectra. Our analysis also shows that the coherence function is influenced by the temporal sectioning of trajectories and demonstrates its applicability to the analysis of Brownian motion.

We investigate the soliton-like wave train solutions of the elevated-order Broer-Kaup system, specifically focusing on its conservation law of exponent 2. We derive the relevant conservation law and determine the dynamic system that governs the wave trains through the Inverse Scattering Transformation. Ultimately, this dynamic system is reduced to a first-order integrable system within the wave envelope, allowing us to analyze the residual dynamics and determine the necessary conditions for the wave trains to stop moving. Furthermore, we examine the dynamics of these wave trains and calculate the work and momentum transferred to the residual dynamics.

This study aims to prove the conservation of energy for the incompressible Euler equations by examining the circular motion of particles. It is well-known that the angular momentum of any individual particle or localized region does not change over time in the absence of external forces. However, this paper focuses on how the circular motion of particles relative to the largest possible circle affects energy conservation. Under specific conditions in two-dimensional space, it is shown that the growth rate of any such circle is directly related to the total angular momentum of the fluid. Using this relationship in the limit where the circle's radius becomes very large, it is shown that the conservation of energy holds true. Additionally, this study extends these findings to three-dimensional space, where the conservation of energy is demonstrated for solutions in circularly symmetric regions.

The Virtual Reality industry is rapidly evolving across multiple dimensions, encompassing advancements in hardware, software, and theoretical concepts such as augmented and virtual reality, passive 3D, and virtual reality applications in physical and virtual environments. This research, spearheaded by VIRTUCOMP, aims to develop innovative VR technologies and devices that integrate seamlessly with standard PCs, in addition to exploring VR content creation opportunities. Two key projects are being developed within the VIRTUCOMP framework, namely VIRUP and VIRPROPS. VIRUP is a software platform allowing users to create photorealistic environments using standard PCs, while VIRPROPS enables users to create and customize their own 3D physical objects. This research paper focuses on VIRUP, discussing its underlying technologies and presenting preliminary findings.

This paper describes a school-based experiment that involved teaching kids about data concepts through hands-on activities with the Data Bricks Expedition (DBE) toolkit. Developed as a tangible representation of data, DBE features movable blocks that can be used to create and interact with data structures like graphs. By integrating DBE in their curriculum, researchers aimed to improve high school students' comprehension of data by comparing it to concrete objects and processes, such as building bricks. Initially, a pilot study with 45 students demonstrated the effectiveness of DBE in enhancing data literacy, particularly in areas like data organization, management, and validation. Following this, a larger-scale experiment involving 434 students further validated DBE's value in teaching data-related skills. By examining the results, it became evident that students developed enhanced data literacy in theoretical areas, as well as their overall understanding of data management principles. Ultimately, the DBE expedition has proven to be a successful educational tool for teaching kids data-related concepts in a hands-on manner.

In Software Defined Networking (SDN), customizing the network with specialized applications is now possible, thanks to innovative use of data-paths.  A novel approach to customizing the network is proposed, allowing developers to easily create customized data-paths by leveraging a graphical software defined networking (SDN) environment.  Within this environment, developers can create and define customized data-packets in a visual and logical sense, without being bogged down by the technical aspects of programming.  To create and define these customized data-packets, a network of data-paths is created with ease, allowing developers to easily create and define these customized data-packets and to customize the network with applications that require specialized traffic patterns.

Weakly untangled representations are a type of disentangled representation, where domain structure is preserved by separating semantic factors from trivial factors. This structure is typically captured in data sets using relational information. However, most methods for learning disentangled representations in supervised settings disregard relational information. To address this, we introduce a new framework that leverages supervised relational data to learn weakly untangled representations. By utilizing supervisory pairs that include both state descriptions and relational data, the model is able to accurately predict relations using relational information and validate them with state descriptions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively combines state and relation information to learn disentangled views, using synthetic and 3D mesh datasets as examples.

The efficiency of a wind turbine with tandem blades can be influenced by the interaction between the blades, with nearby blades experiencing unique wake conditions. A study examined this effect by analyzing the performance of two tandem blades at specific spacing. The blades feature curved tips designed to minimize energy loss caused by the trailing edge. Video from a water-based wind turbine model was used to track the motion of both blades, with computer simulations employed to model the surrounding wake. The investigation focused on the relationship between the blades' motion and wake conditions, with the aim of understanding the optimal spacing between the blades. It was found that increased spacing between the blades led to a more complex interaction, with the tip of the trailing blade experiencing increased load due to the influence of the preceding blade's wake. The findings suggest that tandem blades spaced at 1.9 to 2 blade chords perform better than those with nearby spacing, with the optimal spacing being a balance between the benefits of closer blades and the negative effects on performance.

To study particle physics via real-time lattice QCD, one must first construct a physical observable from fundamental fields. Building on a Bayesian approach to Bayesian estimation, we developed a method to construct a physically meaningful bivariate real-time two-particle correlation function by combining electron field and quark field bivariate real-time one-particle correlations. This approach was validated by comparing the resulting correlation function with a similar one derived from traditional methods. Future work can extend this technique to analyze more complex observables.

The phenomenon of charge-tunneling between a quantum system and a superconductor is crucial for the development of quantum devices. However, the process's underlying mechanisms are not yet fully understood. In our study, a novel approach is introduced where the backscattered current, resulting from quantum interference between different quantum paths, is measured in a device consisting of a quantum point contact in a nanowire coupled to a superconducting domain. By varying the length of the superconducting domain, the time it takes for Cooper pairs to tunnel is altered, resulting in observable effects. In contrast to the predictions of the single-phonon emission mechanism, our data show that the process is primarily driven by multiphonon processes. These findings pave the way for further investigation of the tunneling process in quantum devices where superconductors play a key role.

In the field of chemistry, the primary objective is to develop highly effective and safe drugs through a process of trial and error.  Traditional approaches to drug discovery involve searching and testing numerous molecular structures using a reward-based learning framework.  Nevertheless, the vast molecular pool contains only a small fraction of viable candidates, resulting in excessive costs associated with experimental trials.  In this research, we introduce an innovative framework that leverages generative models trained on an energy-based loss function to circumvent the issue of unexplored structures during the search process.  By utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with a conditional label, we generate target-oriented molecular structures.  Furthermore, we introduce an energy-based loss function to evaluate and optimize the generated candidates, thereby accelerating the search process.  Notably, our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach yields superior results compared to conventional methods, with notable improvements in accuracy and reduced computational costs.

Our research focuses on analyzing user interaction patterns within the online gaming platform, Steam, by examining the network formed by users and tokens used in their interactions, as documented by the Energetic Geometry project. We develop a comprehensive dataset of token-directed graphs derived from six months of steam chat token activity. We then create a user embedding by applying node2vec to a user token graph, enabling the representation of users in a two-dimensional space that is informed by their past token insertion behaviors. We utilize this representation to develop a machine learning model that can predict user engagement levels based on user embeddings, offering a potential alternative to models relying solely on content information. We achieve promising results, indicating that the classification framework has the potential to enhance our grasp of users' interaction behaviors and promote a deeper understanding of engagement dynamics within online platforms.

The Large Magellanic Cloud's (LMC) outer halo's structure and formation history are shaped by its satellites. A study analyzed the movement of the LMC's outer halo stars, using data from VVV and VMC, to better understand its evolution. A sample of around 6000 stars was used to determine the movement of the LMC's outer halo stars, revealing a rotation speed of 78 km/s within a 4 kpc radius. This indicates the LMC's outer halo is rotating, but this speed is lower than the speeds observed in the disk and bulge. A comparison of the LMC's outer halo stars with those of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) showed a similar rotation speed, suggesting the LMC and SMC are likely rotating together, rather than independently. This implies the LMC and SMC began their interaction at least 2.5 billion years ago, in a slow and distant encounter.

A pressing issue in smart grid technology is the phenomenon of power theft, which poses a threat to both the grid's reliability and consumers' security. Identifying power theft incidents in a real-time framework is a pressing challenge. To address this, a novel machine learning-based system is presented in this study. The proposed system leverages smart meter data to identify power theft through a combination of data preprocessing and a machine learning algorithm. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a comparative study of four different machine learning models, and the most suitable model is identified. To enhance model interpretability, a post-processing technique is employed. The results of this study indicate that the proposed system exhibits high accuracy in detecting power theft (99.1%) and determining the duration of the theft (0.85-hour average error margin). Moreover, a comparative analysis with two existing machine learning models reveals that the proposed system outperforms them in terms of detection accuracy and average error margin.

This research paper delves into the geometric implications of homotopy theory, focusing on the interplay between loop spaces and compact surfaces through the lens of iterative connectivity. Key findings include the introduction of loop spaces with a compact graph structure and an innovative construction of loop spaces featuring a compact surface with an embedded graph. Furthermore, this study shows that any connected, compact graph can be embedded in a compact surface if the graph's number of vertices is limited to twice the number of its vertices or edges.

The $D^{0}$ baryon's lifetime is assessed through measurements of $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons produced in $p +$ Cusively separated data, which were obtained from $p$A  collisions at 27 GeV. The lifetime of $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ is estimated to be 6.96 to 8.7 femtoseconds with an error margin of 0.17, and the lifetime of $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ is estimated to be 1.52 to 1.75 times 10 to the power of -22 seconds with an error margin of 0.11. The results are based on a comparison with data separated according to the number of produced charged particles, and the results match previous measurements. The results are also used to determine the ratio of $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ to $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons produced in $p$A  collisions to be 1.20 to 1.45. The results are based on a comparison with data separated according to the number of produced charged particles, and the results match previous measurements.

A new approach to categorize images in the absence of supervision, specifically in the field of hyperspectral images, relies on the assumption that images from the same category share similar patterns. This assumption enables the extraction of categories based on the similarity of features within a feature space. This paper presents a new technique for subspace clustering, combining the advantages of the K-Means algorithm and the Spectral Clustering method, with the addition of a non-parametric distance assessment mechanism. This method, with its modular design, offers flexibility and can be easily applied to various applications. Experimental results using real-world datasets demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency.

The Arctic's sea ice is covered in snow that modulates heat transfer and affects the formation of new ice. A two-layer model consisting of smooth and uniform sea ice beneath a uniformly packed and rounded snow layer was developed to simulate the formation of snow mounds. Numerical simulations of this model accurately predicted the snow distribution in the Arctic as observed by NASA. A simple model of snow accumulation and the movement of snow over uneven surfaces effectively explained the formation of complex snow patterns on the Arctic's sea ice. This model also predicted that the snow's pressure and the temperature at the sea ice-snow interface increase linearly with the thickness of the snow layer.

We investigate dynamic influences on ultracold atom-molecule collisions within magnetic fields that change rapidly. Our analysis reveals a quantum Zeno effect occurs when the influence of these fields is selective, preventing inelastic collisions from occurring by continuously monitoring the magnetic field's properties. However, for faster and faster field modifications, the Zeno effect's effectiveness diminishes, ultimately leads to the inelastic collisions resuming. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations based on exact solutions. Utilizing a unitary perturbation transformation, we successfully derive an effective Hamiltonian to describe the selective dynamic quantum Zeno effect. Our discovery may lead to the creation of novel, efficient, and selective quantum control methods for cold atom-molecule interactions under dynamic magnetic fields.

This paper explores the connection between It\^o-Langevin mechanics and nonextensive thermostatistics. It proposes a quantum-mechanical model describing the motion of a single particle within a confining potential under the influence of stochastic heat transfer. This model is well-suited for simulating the behavior of individual particles in a quantum-degenerate ultracold gas. The calculation of the particle's steady-state momentum distribution reveals a dependence on the heat-bath temperature and a power-law deviation from equilibrium that is consistent with Tsallis' extensive research. This model is further generalized to account for finite particle mass and is found to produce a similar power-law behavior. The resulting momentum distribution functions are derived for both massless and massive particles in a quantum-degenerate regime.

We have identified a new type of nodal-line semimetal in a compound called Co$_3$SnS2 that can be triggered by light. The material's unique response to energy levels allows for the creation of advanced, high-performance devices. The potential for forming intricate topological structures, known as Weyl points, is also present. By examining the properties of the material, we found that multiple types of energy points can be created through a process called type-II Dirac bands. The presence of these points can be confirmed through a specific measurement, and their topological structure is determined by the material's energy points and symmetry patterns. The creation of these points opens up possibilities for the development of novel devices that utilize light.

The increasing demand for decentralized computing is driving the need for developers to deploy their applications on various blockchain platforms, such as DCBET and DAppChain. However, current blockchain-based computing platforms are limited in their ability to seamlessly integrate with existing programming languages and share computing resources. Furthermore, the current state of the market is characterized by high transaction fees, poor performance and low transparency, making it challenging for developers to identify the most suitable blockchain platform for their needs.

In this context, we introduce Marvel DC, a cutting-edge, blockchain-driven, decentralized, and reward-compatible distributed computing framework that leverages a Double-ended Queue-based strategy to ensure that task requests are efficiently processed by miners, thus enhancing system performance and transparency. Specifically, Marvel DC is designed to support a wide range of decentralized computing applications, including those written in diverse programming languages, and features a transparent and efficient smart contract system that minimizes runtime overhead. Moreover, Marvel DC is equipped with a pioneering, decentralized, and transparent computing system that enables multiple miners to participate in the mining process, thus reducing transaction fees and improving the performance of the system.

Through a series of rigorous testing, we demonstrate that Marvel DC is capable of handling a wide range of decentralized computing applications in real-world scenarios, and outperforms existing blockchain-based computing frameworks in terms of system performance, transparency, and transparency.

This research introduces a new framework for assessing 3D point cloud compression systems using Diminished Reference, allowing for a more accurate subjective assessment of quality. The framework's application is specifically relevant to the multi-view video plus depth compression standard, where 3D point cloud information is derived from depth maps. We propose a method to dynamically adjust the number of color points in the reference point cloud based on the number of points in the distorted cloud, resulting in significant time savings in subjective testing. Moreover, our framework enables the creation of training data for deep learning-based predictors of perceptual quality, enabling their evaluation without modifying the reference point cloud. We apply our framework to evaluate the Diminished Reference-based predictors, revealing that they outperform traditional reference predictors.

We utilize the improved holographic model to recreate the QCD phase map defined by the chiral chemical potential. This phase map can identify the phase boundaries between the normal hadronic phase and the quark-gluon plasma phase as well as the strange baryonic matter phase and the strange quark matter phase. Our findings align with existing theoretical predictions and some experimental results. Furthermore, the proposed holographic model offers a way to derive universal dynamical phase transitions for expanding hadronic matter and quark-gluon plasma states.

The Self-Supervised Learning approach has gained significant attention in medical imaging due to its ability to utilize unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Despite this, the method faces limitations in processing MRI data, particularly its low-quality segmentation predictions for irregular structures. This study proposes a novel approach, named SB-SSL, which leverages Self-Supervised Learning for knee irregularity classification using MRI. The method incorporates a novel technique, called Slice-Driven Transform, to create new, transformed slices that enhance the accuracy of prior representations. This is combined with a Self-Guided Transformer, which uses the improved representations to refine the model's feature extraction. The proposed method was tested on 1,520 knee MRI scans and shown to outperform existing SSL methods, with significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, with the code and results available for access.

Creating a classical typeface involves a labor-intensive process requiring
design expertise. However, with the proliferation of digital devices, there's a growing need for user-friendly and cost-effective solutions to produce high-quality typography. This paper presents a few-shot learning method that enables the creation of classical typefaces with minimal example inputs. Our approach enables users to leverage a vast library of pre-defined fonts to facilitate typeface design. This design framework is based on the concept of learning from existing styles to produce new ones, utilizing only a limited number of examples per style. Our model incorporates a cross-domain translation component and a style guidance system to produce rich visual details in characters. Using our system yields impressive results, surpassing existing top-performing methods in this domain.

In equilibrium, fluids exhibit unique properties, such as negative or anomalous values for the shear modulus, which are linked to the presence of non-zero vorticity. These properties, however, are difficult to detect in conventional fluids. We are investigating a class of exceptional fluids characterized by their unusual equilibrium behavior, specifically those that defy conventional descriptions. We have found that the shear modulus of these exceptional fluids can be zero, positive, negative, or anomalous, and the shear modulus's temperature dependence can be unique. We have also determined that the fluids' equilibrium vorticity follows a specific, non-zero distribution and that the fluids' heat conductivity and heat capacity behave abnormally in response to temperature changes. These findings indicate that the exceptional fluids have the potential to exhibit novel properties, such as the presence of negative normal stress, finite shear viscosity, and the manifestation of the Gr\"{u}neisen relation in their thermodynamic behavior.

The growing demand for diverse content on adaptive video streaming is driving the need for effective quality of experience (QoE) optimization. A key obstacle to implementing standard QoE optimization methods within video streaming systems is the lack of accurate representation of user devices. To bridge this gap, we present a digital twin assisted approach for adaptive video streaming QoE improvement. The approach leverages digital twins of user devices to provide precise representations of their hardware and network configurations. These digital twins enable personalized video quality offerings, which are designed to enhance QoE for each user. The personalized video quality offerings are generated using a combination of QoE models, network network QoE models, and machine learning algorithms. To ensure the seamless integration of this novel approach into existing adaptive video streaming systems, we propose a dynamic optimization framework. The framework aims to maximize user satisfaction by allocating personalized video quality offerings under strict storage and bandwidth constraints. The optimization problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-linear program, which is solved using a two-stage approach involving a greedy algorithm and a mixed-integer program solver. The performance of our approach is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed optimization framework. The results show that our approach can effectively improve QoE for each user while adhering to given storage and bandwidth limits.

KM3NeT's underwater optical detector, used for studying neutrinos and cosmic rays, faces a significant challenge with light loss in the 180-m long water segments between modules. To counteract this issue, we have developed a novel double cascade restoration technique for the 1-40 MeV energy range of neutrinos. Our innovative method employs a two-tiered approach, using a first cascade and a subsequent inverse GeV sample to accurately reconstruct neutrino energy, thus significantly reducing systematic uncertainties and enhancing sensitivity compared to the conventional single cascade method used. Simulation results validate the potential of this innovative double cascade technique, especially for analyzing neutrino events within the 1-10 MeV energy range that are particularly challenging for conventional methods.

We examine the generalized nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation under a dispersive condition represented by the differential operator $[1 + \varepsilon(a(t)\cos(2\pi x), b(a^2(t), b(a^2(t), b(a^2(t))]$. With a specific form of the function $a(t) = 1 + \cos(\lambda \sin(t)),$ where $\lambda$ is sufficiently large and the parameter $\varepsilon$ is small, we investigate well-posedness for the associated PNS on a torus $\mathbb{T}$ and on a bounded interval $\mathbb{T}^L$. Our analysis reveals that for a range of parameters, specifically $\varepsilon < \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ for $\lambda \geq 4$, scale-invariant Sobolev spaces play a crucial role in the well-posedness theory, in contrast to the conventional role of Holder continuity. This work also extends scale-invariant Sobolev space theory, incorporating random noise and a non-integrable function within the noise.

This research presents a collaborative approach to scheduling and encoding for ensuring reliable, latency-sensitive data transmission over multiple separate wireless connections. Data is split across these links to prevent data loss in case one link fails, but this also introduces additional delay. Our goal is to find a balance between maintaining data integrity, adhering to strict latency limits, and optimizing throughput. We model the scheduling and encoding process as a mathematical optimization problem, which we then solve using an algorithm that adapts to dynamic link conditions and data demands. Our solution provides a comprehensive framework for adapting to changing network conditions and data needs.

Recent research suggests that the central black hole, Sgr A*, may have been significantly influenced by a massive star explosion, known as a hypernova, which occurred approximately 4 million years ago. This event likely propelled gas and dust towards the Galactic center, creating the central star cluster and shaping the Sgr A East radio source. Various theories have been proposed to explain how the Sgr A East radio source was formed, and our study aims to determine the location of the stellar explosion that led to its creation. Using a novel method, we have analyzed the distribution of stars surrounding the Sgr A East radio source and found strong evidence supporting the hypernova hypothesis. Our results suggest that the stellar explosion likely occurred at a distance of approximately 0.65 parsecs from the Galactic center, and we predict that the Sustained winds from the explosion's progenitor star should have been captured by the Sgr A* potential well. This finding provides further evidence for the hypernova hypothesis and suggests that the progenitor star was a massive star with a mass loss rate of approximately 10^-3 solar masses per year.

We explore the effects of a two Higgs doublet model with a high-beam collision on Lepton flavor equality. Our analysis involves a wide range of operators in both dimensions five and six. By using minimal flavor violation, we obtain the most general form of flavor structure and constraints from low-energy observables such as tau decay processes. Our results indicate that the most stringent limits come from the decays of charged leptons, while the most promising lepton flavor violating decays are those involving beta decays. We also investigate the impact of a high-beam collision on Lepton flavor violating decays, showing that it could be a thousand times more sensitive than current experiments. Our analysis includes a comparison with existing constraints from charged lepton flavor violating decays, as well as a discussion on the potential of a high-beam collision experiment at Fermilab.

This research paper presents our system, DisCoDisCo, that excelled in the collaborative task by the DISRPT2021 community. We introduce a unified approach that integrates discourse segmentation, segmentation categorization, and sentence connection analysis. We leverage a pre-trained BERT model to enhance sentence-to-sentence relationship representation and adapt it for multiple output formats. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across three key evaluation metrics, showcasing the robustness of our system. A qualitative analysis of our results highlights the merits of our method.

The integration of 5G and Internet of Things technology has led to the development of smart cities, but it also highlights the need for ongoing infrastructure development in urban areas. To address this, we propose a new approach, Blockchain-Enabled Architecture for Trusted infrastructure Sharing (BEAT), which allows multiple stakeholders to share shared infrastructure in a secure and transparent manner. BEAT combines the principles of blockchain, smart contracts, and QoS contract theory to facilitate trusted infrastructure sharing. In our model, a network service provider manages a network and enforces the quality of service (QoS) for each service contract. Meanwhile, a blockchain platform serves as a central hub for recording and verifying the agreement between network service providers and infrastructure owners. Our proposed model ensures that infrastructure sharing is reliable, secure, and private. The BEAT architecture is demonstrated through a case study in network slicing and the performance of the model is evaluated through a simulation of various scenarios.

Two-dimensional flow properties can be assessed using the Okubo-Weiss criterion, which determines the rotational and compressibility deformations of velocity gradients in 2D fluid flows. This criterion identifies regions of laminar instability associated with rotating shear flows and is applicable to geophysical and biological fluid flows. For magnetic 2D fluids, an analogous criterion has been derived to evaluate the rotational and baroclinic instabilities influenced by the magnetic field. This study aims to establish a systematic approach for formulating the Okubo-Weiss condition in both electrically conducting and non-conductive fluids, and to demonstrate that it reduces to a specific form for incompressible flows. Furthermore, it presents analytical solutions representing quasi-2D laminar jet and shear flow dynamics across different fluid types.

This study investigates the thermodynamic consequences of incorporating Lee-Wick fields into the early universe when it was first formed. The introduction of these fields alters the universe's initial thermal equilibrium, and we examine their influence on the universe's subsequent thermal evolution. We assume that these fields initially had the same temperature as other fundamental particles but had an effective dimension of $-1$ and utilized supersymmetric models for this analysis. The models we examined, which include both N=1 and N=2 supersymmetry, provide distinct insights into this phenomenon and reveal a thermal separation between the Lee-Wick fields and the rest of the particles in a specific temperature range. Outside this range, these fields behave like normal particles, and we find that their effects on the universe's thermal balance are minimal, leading to a minimal impact on the universe's structure and cosmological features, particularly during the inflationary era, when these fields were ineffective.

Recent studies have successfully employed Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to perform style transfer, but these models often struggle when handling large, high-resolution images due to memory constraints. This paper proposes an innovative solution by utilizing the Transformer architecture to perform style transfer without the need for attention matrices, thereby eliminating spatial indexing and significantly reducing computational costs. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments and expert evaluations, showing it surpasses current state-of-the-art models across various metrics and user assessments, particularly in high-resolution image styling tasks.

The maximum efficiency for erasing any initial state qubit is achieved when a system undergoes maximum entropy production during the erasure process, according to the Jarzynski principle. To investigate this concept experimentally, we analyzed the efficiency of erasing an unknown qubit state in a superconducting circuit coupled to a resonator under various thermal conditions. Our findings support the idea that the highest efficiency occurs when the system is driven by the maximum entropy production rate. Furthermore, our experiment confirms that the inverse of the relaxation time constant is the optimal entropy production for erasure, demonstrating the validity of this principle and providing new insights into the connection between thermodynamic distances and the maximum entropy production.

The production of a single vector-like top quark $T$ at the future $e^{+}e^{-}$ International Linear Collider is being studied under the SM2+1 scenario. To determine the mass and decay mode of the $T$ quark, two advanced analysis methods are being applied to data collected at 250 GeV and 500 GeV, respectively, with integrated luminosities of 1 ab$^{-1}$. These methods are based on the pair production of $Z'$ bosons, which then decay into $T$ quarks via the Drell-Yan process.

The authors examine the stability of non-uniform, non-isentropic fluids under the influence of a sonic field, utilizing the linearized Euler-Poisson equations to describe the system. By applying the Vakhnenko-Boussinesq equation to study long-wave instability, and the Korteweg-de Vries equation to study the quadratic nonlinear stability issue, it was found that the potential for instability exists. Furthermore, the nonlinearity of the Korteweg-de Vries equation was found to be crucial in maintaining stability in the system.

Building upon previous research, specifically weighted shifts on semi-trees described in arXiv:1506.02793, this work extends those findings by generalizing conditions and introducing new weighted shift operators, effectively creating weighted shifts on semi-trees with distinct characteristics. By doing so, this research enables the exploration of diverse weighted shift dynamical systems, even those that don't necessarily belong to the original class. We also enhance existing results, incorporating weighted shift operators, previously proven to be similar to subnormal operators, into a broader category of similar operators, thus expanding our knowledge.

We are proposing an innovative approach to demonstrate the generation of electron-positron pairs by irradiating a high-density high-Z target with an extremely powerful, gamma photon beam produced by a high-power laser operating at a wavelength of $λ^3$ ($\sim300\,nm$). The gamma photon beam produced has a substantial probability of interacting with the target, resulting in electron-positron pair creation. By employing a high-Z target of $\rm Ta_2Se_5$ or similar materials, it is possible to create long-lived, high-energy nuclei that decay into electron-positron pairs, thus generating a dense, two-beam plasma. This plasma can be harnessed to produce a high-power, double plasma mirror soft X-ray laser system, which can be used for future soft X-ray laser development.

In the field of event recognition, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have proven effective in modeling complex event graphs. However, the inherent limitations of traditional GCNNs prevent them from capturing the full potential of graph data, especially when dealing with intricate structures. To address this issue, we introduce two innovative concepts: gate variety and syntactic significance, which enable GCNNs to extract more discriminative and meaningful information from graph data. Furthermore, we derive a novel loss function based on these ideas, which we incorporate into the GCNN framework. Experimental results from various datasets confirm the state-of-the-art performance of our proposed approach.

We examine the problem of Bayesian EIV regression within a Bayesian framework, utilizing a noninformative prior distribution known as the JZ priors. We propose a novel Gibbs sampler based on stochastic approximation and adaptive random walk techniques to facilitate efficient sampling from the posterior distribution. We prove the accuracy of sum-convergence for this sampler and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through both simulated and real-world data analyses.

The precision of optical sensors that utilize multi-qubit systems from diamond or germaniumium enhanced by continuous feedback is significantly affected by the interactions between qubits. To investigate this, an analysis was conducted on a coupled chain of $2n$ particles in $2n$ optical modes, using a specific method to determine the precision limits of the sensors by calculating the Heisenberg limit. The study found that by adding specific noise-decoupling pulses, known as $\sigma^0$ pulses, the interactions between qubits can be minimized, leading to a significant reduction in the precision loss caused by these interactions for all values of $n$. This approach allows for a substantial improvement in the precision of optical sensors that utilize multi-qubit systems with weak inter-qubit interactions.

This paper introduces an innovative, low-rank approximation method for estimating nonlinear dynamical systems affected by random disturbances. By applying the Krylov subspace technique, our approach seeks to identify the underlying stochastic nonlinear structure through two distinct models - ARMA and autoregressive recurrent neural network (ARRNN) - which capture the stochastic noise by incorporating autoregressive lag parameters and recurrent neurons. However, the ARRNN model is more effective in modeling both nonlinear and stochastic dynamics due to its ability to adjust lag parameters and capture hidden data correlations. To demonstrate the superiority of our proposed technique, we utilize the Monte Carlo Monte Carlo method to evaluate and compare its performance in terms of estimation accuracy against the autoregressive linear model, yielding significantly better results.

This research outlines a mathematical framework to calculate the speed of wave transmission within materials that scatter but exhibit nonlinear energy loss properties. By applying this framework, relevant mathematical equations can be formulated for spatially averaged wave behavior in heterogeneous media. The study achieves its goals through a rigorous analysis of the long-term behavior of numerical models for describing such wave phenomena.

Recent research has focused on understanding the decision-making process in deep reinforcement learning (DRL), a field known for its opacity, by developing methods to analyze decision-making. These approaches aim to reveal how models interpret their surroundings and make decisions, yet they often come with the cost of reducing the accuracy of the model by imposing a limited number of constraints. This work introduces a novel method that allows agents to have a high number of interpretable constraints without sacrificing decision-making accuracy, all while providing transparency into how the agent's state is calculated. Our study on the game of Tetris demonstrates that this method can successfully analyze complex actions as composed of fundamental components, and our analysis indicates that most of an agent's decision-making is driven by its ability to effectively interpret its surroundings.

We offer a unified algebraic framework for examining lattice-valued logics based on Boolean algebras. This framework is built upon an expanded semantic framework for logics utilizing Boolean algebras within a specific category of lattice structures. This expanded framework is then used to define a language and prove its expressiveness in capturing lattice-valued logic truth assessments. The connection to specific logic systems is demonstrated through translations, and we identify which formulas from our logic correspond to those in single-variable multi-valued logics. The expressiveness of multi-valued logics is shown through translations, and we also present translations, expressiveness results, and soundness and completeness proofs for lattice-valued fuzzy propositional system logics.

The signature of a stochastic process can be broken down into a Wiener chaos decomposition, which offers a comprehensive understanding of its distributional evolution. Leveraging the existing relationship between Wiener chaos expansions and Mallat's wavelet expansions, we establish a direct link between the Wiener chaos decomposition and the distributional evolution of a Gaussian stochastic process, expressed through wavelet coefficients. Specifically, these wavelet coefficients are defined as the linear predictions of the quadratic form associated with the process's local variance, evaluated at every scale and location. As a result, the Wiener chaos decomposition's preservation of spectral and spatial properties is clearly evident, and the inherent structure of a Gaussian stochastic process is revealed in its wavelet representation.

This research introduces a probabilistic definition of localization efficiency (LE)
in millimeter-wave (mmWave) cellular networks, which is calculated by determining
the percentage of user equipment (UE) that achieve a specified average positioning error, $LE_s$. 
The mmWave channel's location information, known as angle-of-arrival (AOA) and time-of-arrival (TOA), are significantly affected by the large path loss and random fading at each base station (BS), resulting in a high variability in mmWave localization precision across different users. 
To address this, a comprehensive analytical method is developed to assess the mmWave localization performance within a rectangular cell area, where the impact of BS location, antenna height, and user movement on localization precision is analyzed. 
The findings show that the mmWave localization performance is heavily influenced by the user's distance to the BS and its proximity to the optical boundary. 
The presented analysis can be used to determine the required network parameters, such as the base station density, to ensure a specified localization performance, $LE_s$, across the network. 
The results of the simulation experiments confirm the accuracy of the analytical model.

A recently published study has sparked interest in the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, which describes a dilute gas of weakly interacting bosons in an external potential under BEC conditions. The study identified non-uniform solutions with large particle densities at the external potential's core as indicative of a Bose-Einstein condensate, which our investigation also confirms through numerical solutions of the GP equation with randomly initial conditions for a variety of equation parameters.

Recent studies have shown that high-quality image restoration can be achieved by utilizing a two-tiered approach involving both high and low-resolution images. In our research, we further developed this method by dividing the image restoration process into two distinct stages. The high-resolution images are refined first, using a base network to produce these results. The subsequent stage utilizes a second, complementary network to produce the original high-quality images from the restored low-resolution images. The two stages work in conjunction, with the first stage providing guidance to the second through the shared network architecture. The results demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing image restoration methods in both quantitative and qualitative assessments, with the code and supporting materials available online for further investigation.

In the context of bandit algorithms, incorporating additional context can enhance efficiency, but doing so complicates the process. To gain a deeper understanding of this, consider the 'thresholding bandit problem' - where an agent must sequentially select binary actions, each associated with a reward and a 'distractor task' that offers a binary reward. The agent aims to determine not only whether the primary action yields a positive reward, but also whether the 'distractor task' exceeds a predefined threshold. This scenario is a simplified representation of real-world challenges, such as identifying the presence of a specific object in an image. By investigating the properties of bandit problems, researchers have created various classes of thresholding bandit problems, each offering distinct characteristics that can guide the development of corresponding learning algorithms.

This paper delves into a concept first explored by L. J. Stockmeyer in his work establishing a time complexity boundary for logic programming, showing that a broad range of queries can be efficiently reduced to a specific logical framework. The study examines how this result can be achieved and explores its implications, particularly in how it relates to the concept of proof reduction and the relationship between NP and PSPACE. The paper also revisits Stockmeyer's original argument which led to a specific hypothesis regarding the classification of certain computational concepts, aiming to provide a more detailed and rigorous basis for this hypothesis.

This note expands on a previous finding, as stated in Theorem 5.2, and compares the behavior of $H^\alpha$-flows on compact graphs and their complements. Specifically, it establishes that for Hessian-related flows on certain types of compact graphs and their companion graphs, the rate at which they converge to the same form is influenced by the similarity in graphical structures between the two graphs.

A theoretical framework has been developed for analyzing fluctuations in 2D superfluids that exhibit abelian vorticity, with the help of the Coulomb gas sum rule. This rule reveals a link between energy and entropy production in a system, which can be observed in a variety of contexts, including the sum rule in quantum many-body physics and the entropy power inequality in information theory. Building upon this principle, we have derived a formula for calculating the variance of vortex-pair variations in 2D superfluids subject to specific conditions, which can be applied to both homogeneous and non-homogeneous systems. This research also explores the limitations of the sum rule, which fail in certain scenarios, such as when there are no background charges or when the Debye screening length is significantly larger than the interaction length.

Previous studies have examined how people perceive artificial intelligence (AI) in the UK and the US, discovering both similarities and differences in their opinions. This research, however, assesses public opinion about a more sophisticated form of AI, known as Artificial Intelligence 2.0, in an additional 6 countries. Across these nations, the majority of people have heard about AI, but their level of understanding is often limited. Public opinion varies significantly depending on the country, with the UK and US having distinct views on AI, for example, while AI is perceived as a threat in Japan. Notably, AI is viewed as a form of entertainment in the UK and India, but as a form of disturbance in Germany. This study reveals that people's trust in AI is influenced by their political affiliation and that governments play a significant role in shaping people's opinions about AI. These findings have significant implications for how AI technologies are developed and implemented.

A unique decay of the heavy baryon $\Xi_c^0$ to a pion and a $\Lambda_c^+$ baryon has been found to occur infrequently, and we have made the first measurement of its occurrence rate. This decay, which is influenced by symmetry, occurs similarly to a decay observed in the $D^+$ meson, where it breaks this symmetry. The $\Xi_c^0$ to $\pi^-$ $\Lambda_c^+$ decay occurrence rate was measured at $0.106 \pm 0.006$ $\textrm{GeV}^2/c^3$ with uncertainty, using data collected by the BESIII detector.

We establish a solution in Banach algebras for a given equation governing the product of two expressions, lexicographically and implicitly defined. Additionally, this result is utilized to examine the product of two functions, where one function's location is constrained by an inequality and the other varies within a specified interval.

We propose an innovative approach to reinforce learning by integrating the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method within the Actor-Critic model. Traditional Actor-Critic algorithms struggle to find optimal solutions due to random exploration, whereas our new method overcomes this limitation by leveraging the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo technique to perform precise gradient calculations for both the critic and the actor. This enables our model to exploit the learned value functions while taking controlled, informed steps in the direction of the calculated gradients. We present theoretical bounds on the model's expected improvements and demonstrate the efficacy of our method through high-dimensional policy search experiments, which show that it surpasses the performance of traditional Actor-Critic algorithms across multiple scenarios.

We investigate the behavior of light and matter interacting in a complex way within a mathematical framework of three components - one representing light, one representing matter and one representing the interaction between the two. This model is inspired by a quantum model of two photons and two atoms proposed in 1964 by Glauber. In our study, we examine how light affects matter under certain conditions, where each component has the ability to change its state and where the interaction between the components is limited by a certain rule. Through numerical calculations, we find that the system exhibits unique quantum properties at specific points, where each component has an equal share of light and matter. Furthermore, we find that the system undergoes significant changes when one component's light-matter state changes, triggering a tricritical point, and we discover that the system can be described using a mathematical framework of three components.

In the realm of reinforcement learning, particularly in multi-agent settings, developing
efficient algorithms for collaborative tasks is a pressing concern. We tackle this
issue head-on by addressing two key obstacles: (1) the lack of effective
communication among agents; and (2) the limited availability of training data for
agents with restricted access. To overcome these limitations, we propose a
collaborative transfer learning framework that enables agents with restricted access
to learn from more capable agents. Our proposed algorithm, CAMATL, leverages
level-agnostic transfer learning to facilitate knowledge transfer and adapts
communication at multiple levels to optimize the transfer process. We evaluate
CAMATL in both fully connected and sparse connected settings, demonstrating its
superiority over current baselines.

The integration of robotics and artificial intelligence has led to the development of innovative solutions for complex tasks in various industries. This integration, known as collaborative robotics, involves the use of robots to automate tasks that require precision and efficiency. Particle robots, which utilize swarms of small, simple robots working together to achieve a task, offer a cost-effective and safe alternative to traditional industrial robots. However, their effectiveness depends on their ability to navigate and interact with their environment. This research introduces a novel approach to particle robot navigation, utilizing deep reinforcement learning techniques to enable robots to plan safe and efficient paths in dynamic environments. The proposed framework also enables individual robots to perform diverse tasks, such as picking up objects, by determining the most effective strategies through reinforcement learning algorithms. The experimental results of this research demonstrate its potential in real-world applications, and the accompanying video showcases the efficacy of this framework in navigating and interacting with objects in a physical space.

Using the HARPS-PN spectrograph at the ESO 3.6m telescope, we conducted a study to verify the presence of potassium in the atmosphere of WASP-31b. We analyzed 32 transits of WASP-31b and found that our model of the spectral behavior fitted the observed data. We discovered that the abundance of potassium in the atmosphere of WASP-31b was estimated to be less than 0.3 n/cu. cm with a 3-sigma confidence level. This finding suggests that the atmospheric characteristics of WASP-31b are similar to those of HD 189733b. We also found that the atmospheric characteristics of WASP-31b are not consistent with the hypothesis that the planet experienced a massive impact from a rocky or icy planet.

High-performance computing as a service through cloud services is gaining traction as an alternative to acquiring and managing HPC facilities, but it faces challenges in providing reliable compute resources due to the volatility of memory and processing units.  These issues arise because memory is susceptible to data loss when instances are shut down and units can be terminated at any moment.  To address this limitation, we propose integrating non-volatile memory into cloud HPC services.  A cost-benefit analysis of NVM within NVP (non-volatile processing) shows that it can greatly reduce the financial impact of failures.  Furthermore, we argue that NVP should be incorporated into HPC services to promote reliability, scalability, and long-term stability.

In neuroimaging research, a key task is to identify brain connections that influence behavior, which can be viewed as a machine learning problem using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. A recent approach to achieving high accuracy in classification is graph learning, which creates a graph for each data sample and extracts features from these representations. However, a limitation of prior studies is that they focused on individual subjects, whereas our work proposes a novel approach by comparing the brain connections of multiple subjects who perform the same task, thereby improving both inter- and intra-subject similarity. To address this challenge, we developed Comparative Graph Learning (CGL), a graph learning method that generates graphs for classification using multiple subjects, rather than relying on individual subjects. Experiments on two datasets for two social behavior tasks, the Harvard-Hopkins Oddball task and the Exclusion task, show that CGL outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approach, achieving 72% accuracy in classification from fMRI data that outperforms other machine learning methods, including those using deep learning and graph learning techniques.

Inspired by the Gaussian sum conjecture, this research delves into total sums of the power sums of the binomial coefficients $(1)^s, (2)^s, \ldots, (n)^s)$, where $s$ is a non-negative integer. We will explore connections between total sums and various mathematical objects like the Stirling numbers, the gamma function, higher-order Bernoulli polynomials, and polylogarithms in algebra, as well as the Poincaré polynomials and Euler characteristic in topology. Furthermore, we will discuss a special case of the total sums known as Gauss sums and establish that the total sums of the power sums $(1^n)^s, (2^n)^s, \ldots, (n)^s)$ can be represented as total sums of the binomial coefficients $(1)^s, (2)^s, \ldots, n^s$ multiplied by their respective factors.

The investigation of X-ray Cherenkov radiation in thin films has been carried out using a theoretical analysis and experimental data from various incident angles and X-ray energies. Calculations based on the Fresnel diffraction formulation were performed to determine the Cherenkov angle and were compared with theoretical predictions from previous research and experimental measurements of the Cherenkov angle obtained in this study. Experiments were conducted using a beam line at CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron, with incident X-rays from the PS ring at energies of 5 to 20 keV, scattered off polycrystalline targets of copper, silicon, and aluminum, measured using a detector with a thin beryllium window. Analysis of the angular distribution of the X-ray background showed a clear indication of the Cherenkov effect at low angles in silicon and silicon-fluoride samples, in addition to a similar effect in copper and beryllium samples, measured in their absorption edges. The observed Cherenkov effect in thin targets has been found to correlate with the material's refractive index and the angle of incidence.

In this study, we revisit the UCCA framework's original annotation process, 
blending machine learning and annotation techniques to streamline the annotation 
process for texts of any length, while preserving the high standard of manually 
derived UCCA structures and enabling efficient creation of large training datasets 
for related automatic annotation tasks.

A common method for classifying medical images with limited label information involves training a network to localize abnormal areas, then using this process to develop a classification model.  However, the traditional approach to this method has been found to be ineffective when applied to chest X-rays, as the traditional method has been found to be inconsistent.  To address this issue, we have developed a new network called Self-Directed Multiple Instance Learning (SD-MIL) that can learn to localize and classify chest X-rays without the need for precise segmentation.  Our new network uses a self-directed learning approach that involves a new module that can detect and identify the areas of a chest X-ray that contain abnormalities.  Our new network has been found to be more effective than previous approaches to this method when it comes to both localizing and classifying abnormal areas in chest X-rays.

A widely used approach in evaluating probability distributions is Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, but KL may lead to overestimated estimates when there are multiple density estimations. The Hellinger distance offers an alternative measure that remains within the range [0,1] and is more sensitive to discrepancies between the distribution's peaks and tails. Nonetheless, Hellinger distance estimation is often constrained by the requirement that the series of squared differences between the distribution's components must be non-negative. Consequently, this results in over-estimations of the true estimates, and its associated penalized Hellinger distance may not be suitable for model selection in limited sample sizes. In this context, we introduce a novel, modified version of the penalized Hellinger distance that circumvents this non-negative assumption, while maintaining asymptotic properties equivalent to penalized KL distance. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective in model selection through simulated and real-world data sets, and is also applied to the analysis of gene expression data in a specific type of cancer.

The Prouhet-Thue-Morse word $\omega$ is generated by the sequence $0,1,\ldots$ where each subsequent digit is the complement of the preceding one. We investigate the frequency of two-length character sequences within $\omega$, noting their unique recurring patterns. A similar study has previously been applied to three-length character sequences by A. A. Muchnik in 2005. This short paper presents a proof of a conjecture made by A. A. Karatsuba in 2014, which was previously an open issue, concerning the specific sequence patterns.

In real-world classifier choice systems, the cost of model selection plays a critical role in overall risk, prompting us to introduce a novel approach that optimizes both cost and risk. Building on the success of hierarchical clustering in model selection, our method incorporates cost factors into the model grouping process. This is achieved by utilizing a probabilistic method to form hierarchical groups, where the level of the clustering hierarchy and feature similarity are weighted by prior information about class costs. Experimental results confirm that our method effectively balances risk and cost, outperforming existing model selection approaches.

The data reduction process for the Tianlai Experiment, a time-domain multi-band survey project, has been designed to enhance community research in time-domain astronomy. By merging and refining data from various sources, the data product facility offers scientists a comprehensive and efficient platform. In this paper, we outline the data handling workflow and associated tools of the Tianlai Experiment, emphasizing how it will facilitate groundbreaking time-domain research.

To develop high-temperature superconductors like Nb3S4 and NbSe4, researchers have been studying related compounds with square-planar structures. Although these materials are stable in their monolayer forms, they have limited applications due to their relatively low conductivity. To explore their potential for spintronics, scientists are studying their magnetic properties using density functional theory and a multiorbital Hubbard model. The results show that NbSi2N4 and VSi2N4 exhibit robust ferromagnetic states at zero temperature, while NbSi2P4 and VSi2N4 show ferromagnetic states that decrease with increasing temperature, resulting in a Curie-Weiss behavior. Furthermore, researchers have identified a unique feature in NbSi2N4's susceptibility curve that could be used to determine the polarization of spin-aligned states.

This study develops a family of positive semidefinite, stationary, stationary stochastically continuous, and nonstationary kernels tailored for use on non-Euclidean manifolds. These kernels are based on the Moore-Penrose inverse of non-positively defined functions defined on the interior of a Riemannian manifold. By demonstrating equivalence to the nonEuclidean version of Gneiting and Gentle's covariance model, we establish that these kernels exhibit stochastically constant behavior. We then outline a practical approach to constructing a covariance function from our positive semidefinite kernel, and provide an examination of the associated distributional model.

For a positive integer n, a n-generalized arithmetic progression, denoted as A, consists of expressions $A = \{a + nkb: b belongs to [0, n-1] \}$ where a and b are real numbers, and b belongs to the set of nonnegative integers. A set of these progressions is referred to as a set of n-generalized arithmetic progressions. We aim to determine the atomicity of the positive semigroup generated by a set of these progressions provided that the common lower bound, a, and the common rate of increase b, satisfy the condition that $a/b$ belongs to the set of rational numbers.

The attributable fraction among the exposed (AFIE) quantifies the population share benefiting from a treatment due to its causal effect. It's a crucial metric in decision-making and communication for healthcare interventions. However, traditional approaches require data on the entire study population, which can be unattainable. Researchers have turned to using only the data on individuals exposed to treatment, but this leads to an overestimation of benefits and introduces bias by equating treatment and confounder distributions. We propose a novel approach utilizing case description data, leveraging the observed differences between treated and untreated individuals to assess treatment-free and treated individual risks more accurately. This allows for unbiased estimates of AFIE, demonstrated through simulations under various scenarios. Additionally, we apply this method to a case study on antibiotic use in urinary tract infections, using the case description data from a study published in the British Medical Journal.

Consider the standard base change $X_{K_s}$ of a variety defined over a field without Q-cohomology, such that $X_{K_s}$. For certain fields like an infinite union of finite fields or a finite field, it can be demonstrated that any Néron-Degeneracy locus in $X_{K_s}$ is empty, implying that the relative Picard group remains constant across ramified covers within the finite algebraic case.

A study was conducted to determine how the occurrence of $\Upsilon$(1S), (2S), and (3S) mesons is affected by the production of charged particles in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV. The research utilized data from the LHCb detector, with a total integrated luminosity of 0.41 fb^-1. The results showed that the production rates of charged particles surrounding hard events are directly proportional to the rate at which these mesons are produced in the event. The study also found that the rate at which non-charged particles are produced is not directly related to the rate at which $\Upsilon$(nS) mesons are produced in the event.

This research explores the concept of entropy in a quantum dot with two electrons, examining its evolution over time.  Building on a previous model that described the dot as a three-level system, we extend the model to include interactions with a phonon mode, resulting in a nonlinear dynamics for the dot's occupation numbers.  The resulting dynamics are analyzed using the Kolmogorov backward equation, which describes the time-dependent changes in entropy.  Our findings demonstrate that the entropy evolution is non-linear, which in turn affects the equilibrium state of the system.  Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between entropy and the distribution of occupation numbers in a canonical ensemble, revealing interesting connections.

The original Modulus Theorem by Carleman in 1931 states that the maximum value of a non-constant function's gradient within a compact, simply-connected region of the complex plane is determined solely by its behavior at a single point of the region's boundary. Subsequent extensions were made by Carleman and later others to include non-constant functions with complex gradients, as well as other methods. However, the presented work fails to provide a generalisation to all complex-valued functions with complex gradients. Instead, the authors show the Carleman-Carvalho-Pick-Randol extension only holds true for certain types of functions, namely holomorphic or harmonic ones.

We have examined the $L^2$-norm stability of bright solitons within the discrete nonpolynomial Schrödinger equation, which incorporates both short-range and long-range interactions. Our analysis reveals that soliton stability is contingent upon the ratio of $\gamma^2$ to $\gamma_{eff}$. For $\gamma$ exceeding $\gamma_{eff}$, solitons experience a gradual increase in amplitude accompanied by decreasing stability, culminating in metastable states. Conversely, solitons within the framework of the nonpolynomial cubic NLS or NLS with short-range interactions behave oppositely. We have also determined the bright soliton's size and $\alpha$-dependent stability. Our findings indicate that the longest $\alpha$-dependent stability occurs when $\alpha=1$ and $d=2$.

In this study, we propose novel optimization techniques based on mm methods for solving geometric and signomial problems. These mm methods serve as an alternative to generalized gradient methods and can be applied to optimize arbitrary concave or log-concave functions. Building upon this foundation, we specifically focus on solving geometric programming problems which are characterized by signomial functions that are of particular interest to the field of engineering. Our proposed optimization methods exhibit a sublinear complexity in terms of function evaluations required to achieve stationary points. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of these methods and also supply practical, empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness.

We investigate the Teichmuller dynamics resulting from the action of a component of PSL_2(R) on a space of quadratic differentials, and our work demonstrates that this system exhibits the properties of the Smale spectral theory of dynamical systems. Furthermore, we present a detailed description of the Teichmuller manifolds related to the non-wandering sets of the shift and hyperbolic components of the dynamics. A key aspect of our work involves constructing Teichmuller surfaces from the ergodic components of the dynamics, and our main theorem establishes that these spaces have the structure of the universal Teichmuller space. This research also contributes to the study of the moduli problem by proving that any Teichmuller surface with a fixed genus corresponds to a marked Riemann surface belonging to a free, transitive component of the diffeomorphism orbit of the universal Teichmuller space.

Creating a virtual avatar that accurately represents a real person requires advanced technology. Current methods produce a highly detailed avatar, but only after extensive data collection and processing, a lengthy and costly process. To address this challenge, we present PINA, a new method for quickly creating a customized implicit neural avatar from video captured by a single RGB-D camera, a more approachable and widely available technology. PINA surpasses current state-of-the-art methods by leveraging the spatial-temporal structure within video data. To accomplish this, we propose a two-stage framework that first extracts a person's pose from video data, then utilizes this information to generate a neutral avatar representation.
